items.descriptionOriginal: Moving into a retirement community is a big life transition for many senior citizens. Making the choice to downsize and move into a retirement home is not an easy one that can come with many unknowns. In an Reddit forum, member @common_grounder posed the question: “Anyone who’s downsized and moved into a retirement community, what’s the adjustment been like for you?” They continued, “Has it been hard giving up your former life and belongings? Is a more simplified existence comforting to you? Has being around lots of people who are also old been a net positive or net negative?” 16 honest answers from people who know Older people who have made the transition into a retirement community shared their real and honest experiences for those considering making the move. These are 16 of their most informative and impactful responses. Three seniors playing chess together over coffee. Photo credit: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash “I’ve been in an Independent Living Community for 2 years. I was having some health issues and I needed a place that had on duty staff. I downsized twice. My wife and I downsized from a 3 bedroom house to a 2 bedroom Apartment. My wife developed Vascular Dementia the year before the Pandemic. Eventually she went into hospice and after my 3rd hip surgery in 18 months I moved into Independent Living. My 1st year here my bride of 39 years past on from complications of the Vascular Dementia. When I first got here I participated with some of the outing and events. We get 2 meals a day and I used to do dinner with the same group daily. The Presidential election changed that. I loved the people I sat with. However I was crushed that so many of my older peers voted against their interests. I just turned 70 on D-Day. On the average I’m a “youngster” here. Before the election I constantly helped residents conquer their smartphones be it iphone or Android. Now I order lunch and dinner for me to pick up and eat alone in my apartment. I only venture out now for Dr’s appointments and the occasional family outing . I guess more than any thing I miss my bride of 39 years, 44 together. I’m looking forward that my 29 year old son is getting married in August to a wonderful woman and their future looks bright. I’m grateful technology allows me to talk, text and facetime people I care about. At my age, I don’t have many long time friends still on this plane of existence. Even when I downsized to this one bedroom Apartment I still have too much stuff including Heirloom China in my living room for my son that been here 2 years. Oh I almost forgot. We have a happy hour on Wednesday afternoon. I always go and get a vodka tonic and finger food. I was told by my parents to never drink alone. Doing that one drink a week is me not drinking alone.” – @sapotts61 For many folks, it’s been great “I live in a retirement community and I like it a lot. No exterior maintenance, lots of activities and amenities. Beautifully landscaped grounds and great views from my home. Being around similarly aged people is nice too. I really can’t think of a negative. But the quality of the communities vary. Do your homework before taking the plunge.” – @Entire-Garage-1902 Three seniors blowing bubbles. Photo credit: Curated Lifestyle/Unsplash “My wife and I did it 11 years ago. We sold our 4 bedroom 3 bath 2 story house and moved into a 2 bedroom 2 bath single level house in a 55 and better community. It’s been terrific! We have a resort like pool next to the clubhouse and gym. There are tennis and pickle ball courts, gas grills, a big charcoal grill, sauna and spa. It’s a quiet, safe, well kept neighborhood with friendly neighbors.” – @8amteetime “One month into assisted living. I think it’s going to be fine. Just another life transition like college, being on my own, getting married, having kids, building a career, moving into a bigger showplace house, etc. Just in reverse – everything getting smaller and simpler. Downsizing has been very challenging, getting rid of so many objects that still mean something to us, but won’t mean anything to our kids, and there’s not enough space in our 950 sq ft apartment. Having the staff do all the cooking – food has been quite good! – cleaning, and managing my medications, has certainly simplified our lives. And freed up time for my wife to do things she chooses, not just things she must. Moved to a different state where we knew no one, except our sons and their families, so we’re meeting a lot of new people. Haven’t really clicked with anyone yet, but have a half dozen people we can join for meals in the dining room. Yeah, adjustment is going fine.” – @dnhs47 Some people are going bigger, not smaller “We are UPSIZING when move to a retirement community.” – @FootHikerUtah “We upsized into a 55+ community. Sometimes I miss the age diversity with neighbors but my husband and I are 64, pretty active with previously established friendships, part time jobs, and our family. We like that there is a clubhouse with book clubs, game nights, community dinners and a lovely swimming pool. I feel like it’s a home where we can age in place for as long as possible.” – @Competitive-Ice2956 “I upsized when I moved to a retirement community – my Manhattan apartment was 440 square feet, and my car was in a garage two miles away. Here in Connecticut, I’ve got 1500 square feet plus a basement and garage. I’ve got more stuff than ever.” – @vinyl1earthlink “We’ve been in an over 55 community 8 yrs. I love my little house, all on one floor, lots of storage. It’s a bit lonely when our snow bird neighbors go home for the summer, but the grocery store is less crowded. We’ve had several neighbors die recently, but that’s why they call this Gods waiting room. It’s also worrisome to see neighbors having physical or dementia like issues. We aren’t into the pool scene or golf, but we love the indoor walking track. The entertainment shows are a hassle, gotta get those tickets months in advance. We tried a few day long bus trips but their prices are way too high now. Our community is over 40 yrs old and pre 2020 we had thriving crafts, cards, wood, metal, auto, photo clubs….people in charge of those kind of drifted away during the lockdown and a lot of knowledge and organizational skills to run those programs were lost. It’s very quiet here, most neighbors keep their homes very tidy. I’m in a single family home, I have yearly membership dues but no HOA…those are running around $300 a month. We have a great Facebook page that helps us all stay connected and compare notes. All in all I have zero qualms about leaving my old life.” – @Adrift715 “2/2 1400 sq ft villa. It was hard deciding what to keep and what to get rid of at first, but in the end, it was liberating. I love the fact that we can just lock the door and leave without having to worry about outside maintenance.” – @RowdyRumRunner “I’m in a 55 and over community. It’s a very active community, dances at least 2 per month, bingo on Sunday, movies on Thursday, exercise classes at least 3 per day including yoga, karaoke, cards, swimming…I could go on but you get the drift. No obligation to attend any of the activities but they are available. No meals, this is independent living. I’m really happy here, best choice I made after selling my house. Downside for some is living with rules, some people don’t like picking up after their dogs or speed limits or whatever, my place isn’t super controlling but any rules are too much for some people.” – @Kitchen-Fee-5114 “I like it, being on my own I didn’t want a house with all the maintenance. I have a small apartment so I had to get rid of a lot of stuff, that can be hard but I did it. Where I live there is a lot of activities if you are interested, but it’s independent living and some people like that and some don’t. I have made friends, play cards and always have something to do if I’m bored. One of the things you don’t think of is that you meet people and then they die. That is something that can be hard to deal with.” – @Birdy304 “We downsized from our home we lived in for 35 years to a tiny home (399 sq ft) three years ago. While the community is not age restricted, 95% of the people are retired and at least 65. We live on a lake so I get to fish as much as I want. Wife enjoys a bunch of activities such as water aerobics, arts and crafts and dancing. We travel the park in a golf cart. It’s takes minutes to get from one activity to the next. Overall we love it.” – @Dicedlr711vegas Others found it a lot tougher “I am almost 70. I have downsized hugely. I lived in a retirement community for 4 years from 61 to 65 I hated it!” – @Direct_Ad2289 “It’s a very difficult thing. It sounds simple, correct. But it’s what you make of it in your new life. I used to do warranty work for brand new modular homes. Many are doing just that…downsizing. While working, you wind up chatting with many. The stories would run the whole gamut, from ecstatic to downright miserable. My takeaway if you can afford it was maybe try a couple of years’ lease/rent before committing. Sit on any s to get a feel for it first. It was quite heart-wrenching at times. Should have, could have. There’s mental factors to think of. Your circle of friends may change. Someone other than you could be in charge of your property. Suddenly, there’s not a whole lot you can use those tools on anymore, etc. It’s a tough thing to do.” – @xgrader “I (64M) wasn’t ready for it and my wife and I are moving out. I miss seeing kids and families.” – @MacDaddy654321 Anyone who's downsized and moved into a retirement community, what's the adjustment been like for you? by u/common_grounder in AskOldPeople There’s no one right way to do this Reading through all 16 of these, there’s no single right answer here, some people thrived the moment they unpacked their last box, others are still working through the grief of what they left behind. But a theme runs through nearly every response: the hardest part isn’t the square footage you give up. It’s figuring out who you are, and what you actually want your days to look like, once all that extra space and stuff is gone. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Older people get real about what it’s like to move into a retirement community appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: In July of 2021, Simone Biles withdrew from the team final in the Tokyo Olympics and subsequently withdrew from the individual all-around finals after getting a case of the “twisties” that had the world talking. She received overwhelming support as well as overwhelming criticism for the move, with some praising her for recognizing her limits and others blasting her for not persevering through whatever she’s dealing with. Some people pointed to Kerri Strug, who landed on one foot after vaulting on a severely injured ankle in the 1996 Olympics to help the U.S. win gold, as an example of the kind of sacrifice an athlete should be willing to make for their country. One dad’s post flipped the script But was it really? A dad named Byron Heath shared some thoughts about that fateful day in a viral Facebook post that was shared more than 370,000 times in less than a day. Heath wrote: “This realization I had about Simone Biles is gonna make some people mad, but oh well. Yesterday I was excited to show my daughters Kerri Strug’s famous one-leg vault. It was a defining Olympic moment that I watched live as a kid, and my girls watched raptly as Strug fell, and then limped back to leap again. But for some reason I wasn’t as inspired watching it this time. In fact, I felt a little sick. Maybe being a father and teacher has made me soft, but all I could see was how Kerri Strug looked at her coach, Bela Karolyi, with pleading, terrified eyes, while he shouted back ‘You can do it!’ over and over again. My daughters didn’t cheer when Strug landed her second vault. Instead they frowned in concern as she collapsed in agony and frantic tears. ‘Why did she jump again if she was hurt?’ one of my girls asked. I made some inane reply about the heart of a champion or Olympic spirit, but in the back of my mind a thought was festering: She shouldn’t have jumped again. The more the thought echoed, the stronger my realization became. Coach Karolyi should have gotten his visibly injured athlete medical help immediately! Now that I have two young daughters in gymnastics, I expect their safety to be the coach’s number one priority. Instead, Bela Karolyi told Strug to vault again. And he got what he wanted; a gold medal that was more important to him than his athlete’s health. I’m sure people will say ‘Kerri Strug was a competitor–she WANTED to push through the injury.’ That’s probably true. But since the last Olympics we’ve also learned these athletes were put into positions where they could be systematically abused both emotionally and physically, all while being inundated with ‘win at all costs’ messaging. A teenager under those conditions should have been protected, and told ‘No medal is worth the risk of permanent injury.’ In fact, we now know that Strug’s vault wasn’t even necessary to clinch the gold; the U.S. already had an insurmountable lead. Kerri Strug only did that vault because Bela couldn't do math and realize that they had already clinched it. Also as everyone else said she was literally carried off the podium and handed to Larry Nassar. https://t.co/rp3itKPcK2 — Christine Rousselle (@crousselle) July 27, 2021 Nevertheless, Bela Karolyi told her to vault again according to his own recounting of their conversation: ‘I can’t feel my leg,’ Strug told Karolyi. ‘We got to go one more time,’ Karolyi said. ‘Shake it out.’ ‘Do I have to do this again?’ Strug asked. ‘Can you, can you?’ Karolyi wanted to know. ‘I don’t know yet,’ said Strug. ‘I will do it. I will, I will.’ The injury forced Strug’s retirement at 18 years old. Dominique Moceanu, a generational talent, also retired from injuries shortly after. They were top gymnasts literally pushed to the breaking point, and then put out to pasture. Coach Karolyi and Larry Nassar (the serial sexual abuser) continued their long careers, while the athletes were treated as a disposable resource. Today Simone Biles–the greatest gymnast of all time–chose to step back from the competition, citing concerns for mental and physical health. I’ve already seen comments and posts about how Biles ‘failed her country’, ‘quit on us’, or ‘can’t be the greatest if she can’t handle the pressure.’ Those statements are no different than Coach Karolyi telling an injured teen with wide, frightened eyes: ‘We got to go one more time. Shake it out.’ The subtext here is: ‘Our gold medal is more important than your well-being.’ Our athletes shouldn’t have to destroy themselves to meet our standards. If giving empathetic, authentic support to our Olympians means we’ll earn less gold medals, I’m happy to make that trade. Here’s the message I hope we can send to Simone Biles: You are an outstanding athlete, a true role model, and a powerful woman. Nothing will change that. Please don’t sacrifice your emotional or physical well-being for our entertainment or national pride. We are proud of you for being brave enough to compete, and proud of you for having the wisdom to know when to step back. Your choice makes you an even better example to our daughters than you were before. WE’RE STILL ROOTING FOR YOU!” Sending love to you @Simone_Biles -Team UNITED States of America — Kerri Strug (@kerristrug96) July 27, 2021 Plenty of people felt the same way Many people shared Heath’s sentiment, with comments pouring in thanking him for putting words to what they were feeling. We’re in a new era where our lens of what’s admirable, what’s strong, and what’s right has shifted. We understand more about the lifelong impact of too many concussions. We have trainers and medics checking on football players after big hits. We are finding a better balance between competitiveness and well-being. We are acknowledging the importance of mental health and physical health. We are also more aware of how both physical and mental trauma impacts young bodies. Though Kerri Strug pushing through the pain has long been seen as an iconic moment in sports, the adults in the room should have been protecting her, not pushing her through an obvious injury. And the way this fall of Dominique Moceanu at age 14 was handled is downright shocking by today’s standards. She said she never received an exam for it, even after the competition was over. So wrong. In our sport, we essentially dive into a pool w/ no water. When you lose your ability to find the ground—which appears to be part of @Simone_Biles decision—-the consequences can be catastrophic. She made the right decision for the team & herself. @bisping — Dominique Moceanu (@Dmoceanu) July 28, 2021 Nope — Dominique Moceanu (@Dmoceanu) July 28, 2021 Athletes are people, not machines Athletes are not cogs in a wheel, and the desire to win a competition should not trump someone’s well-being. Elite gymnasts already put themselves through grueling physical and mental feats; they wouldn’t be at the top of their sport if they didn’t. But there are limits, and too often in our yearning for a gold medal, or even for a triumphant Olympic story, we push athletes too far. Now we see some of them pushing back, and knowing what we know now, that’s 100% a good thing. Plenty has changed since then. Bela Karolyi, the coach at the center of Heath’s post, died in November 2024 at age 82. And Biles’s story didn’t end in Tokyo. After sitting out four individual finals, she returned to win bronze on balance beam. Three years later in Paris, she won gold in the team, all-around and vault finals, plus silver on floor, bringing her career total to 11 Olympic medals. She has said she is still undecided about competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Games, but that she’ll be at the Games either way, on the floor or in the stands. This article originally appeared four years ago. It has been updated. items.descriptionOriginal: Saul Levmore and Ward Farnsworth are college professors, so it’s fitting that the title of their new book is a question rather than an answer (beyond that being a fair way to pique interest). Like all good teachers, the authors don’t just want us to learn — they want us to learn how to think . In Should You Tip for Takeout? , they mine the fields of law, economics, philosophy, sports, and rhetoric to present a “tool kit for a more rational life.” Far from being an etiquette guide, it’s instead an invitation to expand the way we look at the world, so we can better understand not only our own behavior but others’ as well. Each chapter uses a common quandary — like whether you should recline your airplane seat or get a second opinion before surgery — as a jumping-off point to introduce heuristics and critical thinking techniques that can be applied to countless other scenarios. The resulting pages offer up food for thought and fodder for lighthearted debates. “One way to think about it is we’re trying to write a book that helps people have more fun having conversations at the dinner table,” Farnsworth explained in an interview with Nice News, noting that discussions these days seem to so easily devolve into political arguments or fear-based speculations about the future. “We thought, ‘You know, there’s a lot of things just in everyday life that are actually pretty interesting to think about if you look more closely at them than most people usually do,’” he said, adding: “What would it mean to really take this one apart rationally? What can you learn about the problem that makes everyday life a little more interesting, and maybe what can you learn about rationality that makes other things easier to understand?” Again, anyone hoping for simple “yes” or “no” solutions to life’s dilemmas would be opening the wrong book. In a chapter called “Should You Keep Looking for a Better Price?,” for example, the authors encourage readers to acquaint themselves with distribution patterns and standard deviations. In another, they demonstrate how one might use the mathematical theory of optimal stopping to choose a romantic partner. (Essentially: View the first 37% of your dates or relationships as a comparison pool, and then pick the first subsequent person who’s better than the best one in the sample cohort.) Photo by Lloyd DeGrane from UChicago Saul Levmore That’s not to say there are no straightforward answers. The title chapter delves into the power we have with our wallets to vote for or against a custom when it hasn’t yet become a norm. If something has become entrenched, it’s likely in our best interest to go along with it, whether or not we agree. In the case of tipping for takeout, the authors say that the verdict is in: It’s the norm, so you should tip what you deem a reasonable amount. And doing so may not matter as much to your pocket as you might imagine. “Think of it as a hidden price hike,” Farnsworth said. “But the good news is that you have something to say about it. You have some discretion on how much you’re going to let that price go up. And that should be considered a welcome thing rather than a bad thing, because the alternative is the price goes up for everybody.” The authors said that simply musing through these kinds of common scenarios can reveal possibilities one may never have considered for why things are the way they are and what alternatives exist. Courtesy of Godine Ward Farnsworth “One broad takeaway to me is that people should experiment more in their own lives,” Levmore said, adding, “I think the book tries to encourage people to imagine how the world could be a little bit different from the way it is.” It may also help expand our empathy, Farnsworth pointed out. “Sometimes looking at life and looking for the rationality in it is a way to be more generous-minded toward other people who appear to just be annoying you at random and may be doing just what you would do if you were in their shoes.” When our conversation turned to the most favorable order in which to be interviewed for a job, the pair demonstrated — perhaps unintentionally — just how the aforementioned dinner table discourse may go. “I think it’s a disadvantage to be the last person,” Levmore said, prompting Farnsworth to disagree: “I generally think you want to go last. You want to go as late as you can.” “They get tired,” Levmore rejoined after Farnsworth elaborated, to which Farnsworth replied, “Maybe,” then added: “There’s no right answer to these questions. We just think these problems that most of us sort of wander through unconsciously, they’re just more interesting when you slow down and really ask, ‘What is the best way to handle this?’”

Οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν διαφορετικά μοτίβα αντισωμάτων που θα μπορούσαν να βοηθήσουν στην πρόβλεψη του ποιος θα αναπτύξει αργότερα τη νόσο του Crohn ή την ελκώδη κολίτιδα, ξεχωρίζοντας ακόμη και τα άτομα που διατρέχουν κίνδυνο πιο περίπλοκης νόσου.
items.descriptionOriginal: A major study has uncovered hidden warning signs of inflammatory bowel disease in the blood up to 10 years before diagnosis. Researchers discovered distinct antibody patterns that could help predict who would later develop Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, even distinguishing people at risk of more complicated disease.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν έναν κρυφό διακόπτη που καίει το λίπος και μπλοκάρει τα νέα λιποκύτταρα
items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν ότι η απενεργοποίηση μιας πρωτεΐνης που ονομάζεται Mitch κάνει τα ανθρώπινα κύτταρα να καίνε περισσότερο λίπος και εμποδίζει την ανάπτυξη νέων λιποκυττάρων. Η ανακάλυψη βασίζεται σε πειράματα σε ποντίκια που έδειξαν αξιοσημείωτη αντίσταση στην παχυσαρκία και βελτιωμένη μυϊκή αντοχή, αυξάνοντας τις ελπίδες για μια νέα προσέγγιση στη θεραπεία απώλειας βάρους.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and prevents new fat cells from developing. The breakthrough builds on experiments in mice that showed remarkable resistance to obesity and improved muscular endurance, raising hopes for a new approach to weight-loss treatment.

Μέσω πραγματικών γονέων, προπονητών γονέων, επιρροών και ειδικών, η σειρά φέρνει ειλικρινείς, διαφορετικές και σχετικές προοπτικές για το q…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. When Aayansh Singh first visited a farm near Mumbai, the horses, pigs and hens he had seen in picture books suddenly had a life of their own. Two years later, he returned with one wish: to ride a horse. For his father, Bhanu Singh, a software engineer based in Mumbai, watching that wish come true was a reminder of how much a child can take away from an experience that seems simple to an adult. "When we first took him, I honestly thought he would forget everything because he was only two years old," Bhanu recalls. "But for the next year, he kept talking about the horses and remembering the farm." It began with a small observation at home. Aayansh, then two, could identify horses, pigs, cows and goats from his picture books. He knew what they looked like, but he had never encountered them outside the pages. What began as a day of discovery became a memory Aayansh continued to talk about long after returning home. "We wanted him to go beyond books and experience them firsthand, to see them up close, touch them, and understand how they feel and behave," Bhanu says. That thought led the family to Japalouppe, a farm they discovered while searching online for a place near Mumbai where their toddler could meet animals. When the pictures came alive The family kept their first outing simple. Japalouppe was about a 1.5-hour drive away, making it manageable for a day trip with a young child . There was no packed itinerary or long list of attractions to tick off. For Bhanu Singh, the experience was a reminder that simple outings can leave lasting impressions on young children. Bhanu was drawn to the farm's open spaces, animals and horses. They also carried some food, unsure whether they would find suitable, non-spicy options for Aayansh. To their pleasant surprise, the farm had a child-friendly menu. Once they arrived, the family let the day unfold at Aayansh's pace. "He didn't run around shouting or get overwhelmed. He was quiet, curious, and busy taking everything in," Bhanu remembers. One moment that stayed with him was watching his son run around the hens. Until then, hens had been pictures in a book. Now, they were moving around him, clucking and going about their business. The horses and pigs offered another kind of discovery. "He looked at the horse like he was thinking, 'This is the horse from my book.' He did the same with the pig. In his book, it was just a picture, but here it had a smell and made a sound. For him, it was a big thing." The family's two visits showed how hands-on experiences can help children build on what they learn from books. For the adults, these might have been ordinary sights and sounds. For Aayansh, they were details that no picture could quite capture. The family stayed close, letting him decide how near he wanted to get to each animal. A dedicated guide showed them how to approach and handle the animals safely, explaining which feed to offer and how to do it. There was no need to hurry him along. If something caught his attention, he could stay and watch. From watching horses to riding one The first visit was about getting acquainted with the animals. Aayansh was too young to ride a horse, but the experience left him with memories he continued to talk about long after the family returned home. Then, at three and a half, he asked to visit the farm again; this time, he had a plan of his own. "He clearly told us he wanted to visit again and ride a horse," Bhanu says. At three and a half, Aayansh returned to the farm with a wish of his own: to ride a horse. The family returned, and Aayansh got his wish. He was the youngest child on the farm to ride a horse that day, making the moment especially memorable for his parents. Bhanu noticed how much had changed. On the first visit, his son had watched the animals with wide-eyed curiosity. Now, he knew what he wanted to do. He approached the experience with greater confidence , going around to meet the animals again, almost as if he were reconnecting with old friends. "For us, the most special part was watching him sit on the horse with so much pride," Bhanu says. "The first trip was about discovery, while the second was about building on those memories and trying something new on his own." A holiday doesn't need a packed itinerary The two visits changed the way Bhanu thinks about family holidays. Earlier, he associated a good holiday with travelling to a new destination and having plenty of activities planned. Now, he finds himself asking a different question before choosing a place: "What will my child actually experience here? What will he see, feel, and remember?" His advice to parents who want to introduce young children to nature is to start small. Choose a place close to home, perhaps somewhere connected to an animal or activity the child already loves, and leave room for curiosity to lead the way. "Don't try to fit too many activities into one day. Let your child explore at their own pace, follow their curiosity, and enjoy the little moments," he says. After all, Aayansh's first farm visit wasn't filled with elaborate attractions or a faraway holiday backdrop. It was a day of watching hens, meeting pigs and standing close to horses he had previously known only from books. For parents, Aayansh's story is a reminder that meaningful family holidays need not involve packed itineraries or faraway destinations. Yet those encounters stayed with him. They even gave him something to look forward to when the family returned. And perhaps that's one of the loveliest things about travelling with children: you may plan the outing, pack the snacks and choose the destination, but you never quite know which small moment will find a permanent place in their hearts. And sometimes, the best souvenirs from a family holiday are the memories a child carries home, and the little adventures they can't wait to have next. All images courtesy of Bhanu Singh

items.descriptionOriginal: Cut open a ripe jackfruit, and you are greeted by its golden-yellow flesh, sweet aroma and sticky, fibrous peel. While the juicy fruit often finds its way into curries, chips and desserts, its thick outer covering usually ends up in the bin. Researchers at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Rourkela , however, have found another use for this often-discarded part of the fruit. They have turned jackfruit peel into a material that removed more than 90% of fluoride from contaminated water in laboratory tests, in about 10 minutes. The idea brings together two things that rarely make it into the same conversation: fruit waste and safer drinking water. For families whose groundwater contains too much fluoride, which can damage teeth and bones over time, this innovation could eventually offer a more affordable way to make drinking water safer. How does jackfruit peel help clean water? The secret lies in what researchers have made from the peel. The team converted discarded jackfruit peel into activated carbon and modified it with zirconium, a metal that helps the material capture fluoride from water. Modified with zirconium, jackfruit-peel-based activated carbon helps capture excess fluoride from contaminated water. Photograph: ( Nature ) Prof. Susmita Mishra, Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering at NIT Rourkela, explains the thinking behind the innovation. "The key idea behind this technology is to use an agricultural waste material as a resource for water purification. We prepared activated carbon from discarded jackfruit peel and modified it with zirconium to improve its ability to capture fluoride from water," she adds. The material showed promising results in laboratory tests, removing over 90% of fluoride within approximately 10 minutes under the tested conditions. Fluoride occurs naturally in water, but drinking water containing too much of it over a long period can damage teeth and bones. This condition, known as fluorosis, can affect both children and adults. Removing excess fluoride, however, is not always straightforward. Reverse osmosis, a widely used water treatment method, can waste considerable amounts of water and remove minerals such as calcium and magnesium. Other methods, including ion exchange and activated alumina, also come with limitations, including the use of chemicals that can raise environmental concerns. The NIT Rourkela team's approach explores whether an agricultural by-product can help make fluoride removal more accessible. What did the researchers find? In laboratory experiments, the jackfruit-peel-based material removed more than 90% of fluoride from water containing around 1–5 milligrams per litre. Under the tested conditions, the team recorded removal efficiencies of over 90–97% within 10–20 minutes. The patented innovation by NIT Rourkela researchers offers a new approach to tackling fluoride contamination using agricultural waste. Photograph: ( Gujarat Samachar ) The researchers have also secured a patent for the technology. The team comprises Prof. Mishra and Dr. Pratima Minz, Research Graduate at NIT Rourkela. They estimate that preparing the material costs approximately Rs 37 per gram, based on the electricity and chemicals used in its synthesis. These are promising early findings, but there is still some way to go before the material can be used to treat drinking water outside the laboratory. The research has reached Technology Readiness Level 4 (TRL 4), meaning the material and its underlying concept have been validated in a laboratory environment. What happens next? For families in rural and semi-urban areas where groundwater contains excess fluoride, an affordable treatment option could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their material could eventually be used in decentralised water treatment systems, bringing purification closer to the communities that need it. Prof. Mishra says, "The potential of this technology lies in its use of an easily available agricultural by-product to develop a cost-effective material for fluoride removal. In the long term, the technology could contribute to water treatment solutions for communities in fluoride-affected regions, subject to further testing and validation." The team is now working towards a prototype to test the material's potential beyond the laboratory. Photograph: ( The Printlines ) The next step is to develop a physical prototype and test how the material performs in practical conditions. The team will also study its long-term performance and operating costs to understand whether it can be deployed on a larger scale. A discarded jackfruit peel is not yet ready to make drinking water safer on its own. But this research offers an interesting possibility: something routinely thrown away could, with further development, become part of a solution to a problem that affects communities across India.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 50-year-old Japanese planting method is quietly reshaping vacant lots, schoolyards, and parking strips across the United States -- not through large-scale industrial effort, but through the hands of neighbors who show up on a Saturday to tuck seedlings into carefully prepared soil. Developed by botanist Akira Miyawaki, the method skips the slow prologue of natural forest succession, mixing climax species and their supporting plants to create self-sustaining ecosystems within decades rather than centuries. What makes it remarkable is not just the science but the ritual embedded in it: "He would take each plant, and the community had to say its name," recalls one organizer -- "it was about restoring relationships between humans and non-humans." The miniforest movement asks something modest of each participant and returns something harder to name: a sense of belonging to a place, and a stake in its future.

items.descriptionOriginal: What does meaningful community collaboration look like? In Bengaluru, Inventure Academy is working alongside government schools to create more opportunities for children to learn, explore and discover their potential. From teachers learning together to students engaging with real-world challenges, the collaboration extends beyond the classroom. Initiatives like Our Voice, Inventurepreneurship and the Change Maker Challenge encourage children to participate in their communities and find ways to make a difference. This work has earned Inventure Academy a place among the world's Top 10 schools for Community Collaboration at T4 Education's World's Best School Prizes 2026. The school is also in the running for the Community Choice Award, decided by public vote. items.titleOriginal: How 2 Bengaluru Designers Are Reimagining Empty Flyover Space With Swings, Seats & Greenery
items.description: Στη διασταύρωση ιπποδρόμου του Μπανγκαλόρ, οι άνθρωποι που διέσχιζαν το δρόμο έπρεπε να περάσουν περισσότερο από όσο έπρεπε ανάμεσα σε κινούμενα οχήματα. Μια στροφή έδωσε στα αυτοκίνητα μια γενναιόδωρη σάρωση του δρόμου, αφήνοντας τους πεζούς να βρουν το δρόμο τους μέσα στην κυκλοφορία. Όταν οι αστικοί σχεδιαστές Nishita Parmar και Vedanti Agarwal μελέτησαν τη διασταύρωση, ανακάλυψαν κάτι εκπληκτικό. Σχετικά…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Bengaluru's Racecourse Junction, people crossing the road had to spend longer than necessary among moving vehicles. One turn gave cars a generous sweep of the road, leaving pedestrians to find their way through traffic. When urban designers Nishita Parmar and Vedanti Agarwal studied the junction, they discovered something surprising. Relatively few vehicles were using one left turn, while far more people needed to cross that stretch. Why, then, was so much space being given to cars? Working with principal designer Monik Shah and the team at Compartment S4 , they helped redesign the junction to include a pedestrian refuge island, giving people somewhere to pause while crossing. The work was part of the Orbital project, commissioned by the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) and supported by the Sustainable Mobility Network. It was one example of a question guiding their work across Bengaluru: how can streets and the spaces around them better serve people on foot? Why did one left turn have so much space? The team began at Racecourse by observing how people and vehicles actually moved. They counted traffic, followed pedestrian routes and noted where the two came into conflict. "When we actually went and mapped that entire junction, we understood that the volume of vehicles coming from [the road] and going towards the left was much lower compared to the volume of pedestrians," Parmar says. That meant pedestrians were crossing a wider stretch of moving traffic than necessary. "We call it pedestrian exposure time. To cross from A to B, it took a longer time, and that means you're getting exposed to the moving vehicle for longer," she explains. The designers proposed a more compact turn, changes to traffic movement and a refuge island to break up the crossing. For someone walking to college, work or another destination, spending less time among vehicles could make the journey easier. This matters at a junction serving the Race Course, educational institutions and other destinations. Students and other pedestrians pass through daily, while events bring larger groups into the area. At Racecourse Junction, vehicles had a generous sweep of the carriageway to negotiate one of the turns. By December 2023, BBMP had begun redevelopment work at Race Course Road junction, including plans for pedestrian crossings, seating and waiting areas. In February 2025, local reporting described the redevelopment as completed, with benches installed for pedestrians and officegoers . Compartment S4 also lists its Race Course Junction project as completed. A road can appear to need more space for vehicles because of the way it has been designed. But once actual movement is measured, the hierarchy can look different. The physical intervention is documented, although published before-and-after figures showing reduced crossing times or traffic conflicts were not available for this story. Why test a design on the street first? Parmar trained as an architect at CEPT Ahmedabad. Her experience in urban design and strategy, including work with Jaipur's Domestic Workers' Union, exposed her to the ways public infrastructure affects everyday lives. Agarwal, who has a Master's in Urban Design from UC Berkeley, has worked on urban mapping, landscape-led planning, transit-oriented development and environmentally sensitive design in India and the United States, including at WRT's San Francisco studio and Studio POD in India. Their approach begins with observing rather than assuming. Before committing to permanent changes, the team tested how a redesign worked on the street. That matters because people rarely move exactly as a drawing predicts. Someone may take a shortcut across the road; a driver may turn differently when traffic builds up. Watching these movements allows designers to identify problems and adjust plans before construction becomes permanent. "The issues never come under one sort of bucket. There is a transport issue, there is a utility issue, there is a space-constraint issue, there is a traffic issue, and everything comes together to form an urban issue," Parmar says. They began looking for locations where one intervention could address several concerns, including awkward road edges and spaces left beneath flyovers. "We started mapping these areas or these locations where there is some kind of demonstration possible to make that a lighthouse project and show how you can think of spaces, otherwise negative spaces or deformed spaces in the city, as something different," she says. Turning such ideas into actual spaces also means working within government approvals, budgets and construction constraints. "If we aim for something really high in the first go, it might not get passed or it might not have the budgets to get implemented," Parmar explains. "Whatever intervention we do, it is not only solving one particular thing, but it is looking at all the aspects of issues in an urban context," she adds. That thinking led the team to Shivananda Flyover. Turning unused flyover space into a public park At Shivananda, a large area beneath the flyover was going unused, while people passing through had barely 1.5 feet of footpath to walk on. The team's surveys showed that pedestrians were already using this route between residential neighbourhoods, universities and the Race Course. The designers wondered whether some of the underused land could become a more welcoming place for them. "The flyover was taking up a lot of space which was unused," Parmar says. "So we thought, let's take this and integrate it with the junction." Their response was Pause Park, designed with seating, platforms, steps, swings, greenery and art. The aim was to give people a place to sit and spend time in an area they previously had little reason to stop in. The area connects residential neighbourhoods with universities and the Racecourse, meaning people were already using it as part of their daily routes. Work to make the area useful was under way by June 2023, when BBMP was constructing benches and public toilets after residents objected to an earlier proposal for a basketball court and skating rink, citing safety concerns around nearby traffic . In February 2025, civic officials described Shivananda Circle among junctions they had developed. However, a report on 31 May 2025 said finishing work on the mini park's swings and greenery was still in its final stages. An exact public opening date, and whether all facilities are currently accessible, could not be independently confirmed. The idea nevertheless poses a valuable question for a city full of flyovers: could the land beneath them offer something useful to the people who walk past every day? Will people actually use these spaces? For road junctions, the team can examine crossing times, traffic flow and potential conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles. "For junctions, it is about seeing how smooth the traffic flow has become. These things are more objective," Agarwal says. The team is also examining how urban design might lessen the effects of heat. After a space is built, they consider post-occupancy studies , returning to see how people actually use it. "For open spaces, it is about going during the most active hour and seeing whether the community has adopted it," Agarwal says. The resulting Pause Park introduces seating, platforms, steps, swings, greenery and art into the space beneath the flyover. Are children playing there? Are older people sitting comfortably? Can different groups share the space? Such observations help show whether a public place is working as intended, and what may need to change. What it takes to get a better street built For the designers, a challenge lies in making the work behind the final design visible. Surveys, conversations with communities and coordination across departments all take time, even if the public usually sees only a finished image. "Research is an intangible component, but it eventually drives the project," Shah says. "The government wants to see the 3D renders." Parmar says many government agencies are more familiar with architecture and structural consultancy than with the process urban design requires. "They don't always understand that arriving at an urban-design proposal needs a different kind of process," she says. The team is therefore working on how projects are commissioned and carried out, including surveys, community engagement, procurement and implementation. "We are helping governments redesign the SOPs for how designers should engage with such projects," Parmar says. At Racecourse, their work began by noticing how much road space was devoted to a little-used turn. At Shivananda, they looked at the people squeezing along a narrow footpath beside a large, underused area. In both places, the first step was the same: pay attention to how people live with the city that has already been built, and use that understanding to make it work better for them. All Pictures: Compartment S4

items.title: Άτομα από τη Generation Jones εξηγούν τις κύριες πολιτισμικές διαφορές τους με τους Boomers
items.titleOriginal: People from Generation Jones explain their major cultural differences with Boomers
items.description: Η Generation Jones, άτομα που γεννήθηκαν από το 1954-1965, θεωρείται μια «μικρο-γενιά» μεταξύ των Boomers και της Generation X. Αν και συνήθως συγκεντρώνονται με τα Boomers, υπάρχουν μερικές αρκετά ευδιάκριτες διαφορές μεταξύ τους. Σε μια διαδικτυακή κοινότητα των Generation Jones-ers, ένα μέλος με το όνομα @WalkingHorse, παρότρυνε όσους στη Generation Jones να συζητήσουν πώς…
items.descriptionOriginal: Generation Jones , people born from 1954-1965, is considered a ‘micro-generation’ between Boomers and Generation X . Though typically lumped in with Boomers, there are some pretty distinct differences between them. In an online community of Generation Jones-ers, a member named @WalkingHorse, prompted those in Generation Jones to discuss how their upbringing differed from Boomers in a post titled “What is and who are Generation Jones. Step inside…”. “We’re often described as pragmatic idealists, raised on big dreams but tempered by economic recessions and a sense of lowered expectations compared to the Boomers’ post-war prosperity,” they wrote. “Think of us a generation that got the tail end of the party but had to clean up the mess.” So, what makes them different? It inspired many Generation Jones members to share their thoughts and opinions. These are some of the major cultural differences those in Generation Jones have with Boomers: “We were too young to fully participate in the counterculture of the ’60s but old enough to feel its aftershocks.” – @WalkingHorse Gen Jones men also signed up for the selective service, but were not drafted as the Vietnam war had ended.” – @tedshreddon “Boomers had Elvis and The Beatles. We had Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd.” – @Scr33ble “First teenage generation to experience the Space Shuttle launch. First teen generation to watch music videos in between movies on cable TV then the birth of MTV. We laughed when hearing that golf obsessed President Gerald Ford would routinely slice or hook a ball into a crowd of spectators. Then laugh at Chevy Chase for mimicking our clumsy commander in Chief. We watched our parents go through the fuel rationing days where you could only buy gas for you car if the last digit on the plate was an odd or even number. We counted days along with the media on how long the Iran hostages were being held. We lost John Lennon while not in that sweet spot age to have experienced the musical British Invasion of the 60’s. Instead, MTV opened to floodgates to the Brit-pop invasion of Duran Duran followed closely by big hair, neon clothing and wondering why saying ‘too hip’ was all that and a bag of chips. Best part was that college tuition was sorta affordable.” – @contrivancedevice There for the start of major social change “Not mentioned yet, but we were present for the rise of gay rights. Went to my first gay bar at 19. Music, especially Disco, was infused with pride and acceptance and coming out. ‘We are Family’, ‘I’m Coming Out’. Queen and the Village People, etc. The rise of ‘women’s music’ like Holly Near and Chris Williamson. Activists like Harvey Milk and later ACT UP. We were young adults when AIDS hit and the fight for treatment led to a huge wave of coming out. We lost a whole generation of gay men to that plague. ” – @BldrJanet “Boomers remember where they were when President Kennedy died. We remember where we were when John Lennon died.” – @KJPratt “Musically speaking, I think we were blessed. Our musical heyday had everything. Our moms played Elvis the king on the radio, and we had Elvis Costello. The Stones and The Who transverse generations. We are old enough to remember Joan Baez and Bob Dylan pre-Chalamet, not to mention Freddie and Elton before their bio-pics. And Johnny Cash too. And shout out to the poster girl of the 80’s Cyndi Lauper (I got special love for her as a race tracker cause she walked hots at Belmont Park.)” – @Binky-Answer896 “We gave a hoot, and didn’t pollute!” – @Awkwardimplemet698 “We are the generation that got to see the war every evening at dinner ‘live via satellite’. – @blurtlebaby “Think: 45s—albums—-8 tracks—cassettes—-CDs—-Streaming! I’ve had the Rolling Stones on all!” – @NOLALaura “I always said that I experienced it all…born in 1957. I listened to my older siblings music. I stole my sisters Woodstock album when she went off to college. I still have it. I recall all the assassinations from JFK and MLK.I saw RFK being killed on live tv.(at least I think I did), I remember the chaos of the Vietnam war, the Chicago riots, the Nixon mess. I recall the beginning of the environmental fight, Sesame Street and the moon launch. Computers, and floppy discs, cell phones that came in small cases that would plug into the car. So much good stuff. So much chaos.” – @mammaV55 “There’s a sure way to know if you’re Gen J. Were you deadly afraid of quicksand?!” – @NOLALaura What is and who are Generation Jones. Step inside… by u/WalkingHorse in GenerationJones A generation still finding its name That’s really the throughline of every response here: a generation that grew up in the gap between two much louder cultural identities, and had to piece together its own story out of half-remembered assassinations, borrowed older siblings’ records, and a war that ended just in time to spare them but not their nerves. Boomers got Woodstock. Gen X got grunge. Generation Jones got the hangover in between, and somehow turned it into its own kind of resilience. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post People from Generation Jones explain their major cultural differences with Boomers appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το κοριτσάκι μπήκε σε ένα talent show χωρίς να το πει στη μαμά του και το πλήθος ήταν εδώ για αυτό
items.titleOriginal: Little girl entered a talent show without telling her mom, and the crowd was here for it
items.description: Ένα κοριτσάκι μπαίνει μέσα στις καρδιές των ανθρώπων και υπενθυμίζει σε όλους μας πόσο σημαντικό είναι να βάζεις τον εαυτό σου έξω κάθε τόσο. Σε ένα πλέον viral κλιπ TikTok που δημοσιεύτηκε από τον @ashleydkennedy14, μαθαίνουμε ότι η ανιψιά της στο νηπιαγωγείο είχε προφανώς συμμετάσχει σε ένα talent show χωρίς να το πει στη μαμά της, κάτι που περιελάμβανε…
items.descriptionOriginal: One little girl is somersaulting her way into people’s hearts , and reminding us all of how important it is to put yourself out there every once in a while. In a now-viral TikTok clip posted by @ashleydkennedy14, we learn that her kindergarten-aged niece had apparently entered herself into a talent show without telling her mom, a feat that involved forging mom’s signature onto a permission slip, no less. And just what did this “act” consist of? Somersaults. Lots of ‘em. Six, to be exact. Also one cartwheel, for good measure. She’d basically deliver one roll, wait for uproarious applause, then do another one. Solid routine, if you ask us. Honestly, it’s hard to tell which aspect of this moment is more endearing: watching this little girl valiantly overcome a wee bit of shyness, and in the process tapping into some pretty captivating stage presence, or seeing how enthusiastic the audience was to support her. Just good, wholesome stuff all around. Watch: Even online viewers were taken aback by this girl’s fearlessness. Or rather, her determination to keep going, in spite of her fear. People couldn’t stop talking about it “I need to know what her parents did because this is CEO level confidence and I am here for it.” “She was like oh u like that ” “Im honestly impressed by her independence. She signed herself up and was confident that she had it. Good job mama.” “She will go far in life. Courage is everything.” Others noted how kind the crowd was to cheer her on. “For the people who clapped, as a mother : THANK YOU. it means a lottt.” “The cheers from the crowd are the best.” “Ok. because the crowd passed the vibe check. We cheer over here, be brave!” Funnily enough, plenty of other folks chimed in with similar stories of kiddos sneaking into talent shows…with talents they may or may not have actually possessed. “My son tried to sign himself up to do karate at his school talent show…he’s never been to a karate class in his life…” “My daughter entered herself into the talent show in 1st grade and didn’t say anything. She played the piano… she had never played piano in her life til that day lol I need that confidence.” “My brother did this! He played harmonica for the whole school. He doesn’t know how to play the harmonica.” The real lesson here is bigger While this girl might receive a stern talking to about the importance of not forging signatures, her story is nonetheless a prime example of how kids can really shine when left on their own to take risks, try new things, and opt for exploration over perfection. It can be hard for parents to not want to protect their little ones from failure (whatever that means), but life often provides moments just like this to remind them that taking a step back is a precious opportunity to help instill some self advocacy. It’s just like the old saying goes, “Leap, and the net will appear.” Or in this case…somersault, and the cheers will follow. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Little girl entered a talent show without telling her mom, and the crowd was here for it appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Skincubator: Επαναστατική συσκευή που επιτρέπει στους γονείς να εξασκούν την επαφή δέρμα με δέρμα με πρόωρα νεογνά
items.titleOriginal: Skincubator: Revolutionary Device Lets Parents Practice Skin-to-Skin Contact With Preterm Newborns
items.description: Η επαφή δέρμα με δέρμα, η πρακτική της τοποθέτησης ενός νεογέννητου απευθείας στο στήθος της μητέρας ή του πατέρα, θεωρείται απαραίτητη - μερικές φορές σωτήρια - φροντίδα για τα πρόωρα βρέφη. Ο Παγκόσμιος Οργανισμός Υγείας το συνιστά για τουλάχιστον οκτώ ώρες την ημέρα από τη γέννηση για όλα τα μωρά που γεννιούνται πριν από τις 37 εβδομάδες. Οι θερμοκοιτίδες μπορεί επίσης να είναι κρίσιμες για τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Skin-to-skin contact, the practice of a newborn being placed directly onto the mother’s or father’s chest, is considered essential — sometimes lifesaving — care for preterm infants. The World Health Organization recommends it for at least eight hours a day beginning at birth for all babies born before 37 weeks. Incubators can also be critical for these newborns, however, and yet the carefully controlled environments prevent parents from performing that crucial skin-to-skin contact. A pioneering new technology has now bridged the two forms of care, allowing parents to hold their babies to their bodies without disrupting the essential treatments they require. Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital The Skincubator is a wearable medical tool designed for preterm infants weighing under 4.4 pounds that enables prolonged skin-to-skin contact beginning as early as the day of birth. A couple at Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston, Texas, recently became the first in the U.S. to experience the difference it can make. For about 10 days after their twins were born in August, Tiffany Ikwuagwu and Dorian Ojemen weren’t able to hold the babies, who arrived at just 26 weeks. “This is a great invention,” Ikwuagwu, herself an obstetrician and gynecologist, said in a video from Memorial Hermann upon using the Skincubator. “I think the fact that I can help regulate the babies’ heart[s] and help the babies relax and just have that connection to them, is very special.” Added Ojemen in an interview with CNN earlier this month: “Just the fact that you can have them on your chest, you can look in their eyes, you can hold them, feel them breathe, like, that immediately makes you feel like, wow, I’m a parent.” The tech, which was developed over four years, was granted FDA Breakthrough Device designation last December. With the Skincubator, parents can relax or rest while bonding with their baby for hours at a time, taking turns with other caregivers and family members if they so choose. Infants’ arterial, umbilical, feeding, and airway tubes all remain in place. “The baby is already in their incubator, and they’re transferred from the incubator to the Skincubator while they’re in their isolate,” explained Dr. Jaclyn Ruggiero, principal investigator for an ongoing clinical trial, adding: “The baby’s medical lines and breathing tubes or breathing support are all secured to the Skincubator base. And the way the baby gets into skin-to-skin care is there’s a retractable pad under the baby, and that pad is pulled down slowly.” Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital Skin-to-skin contact is standard practice for all babies, helping to stabilize their heart rate and breathing, stimulating digestion, regulating temperature, providing protection against infection, and fostering the bond between parent and child. “It turns on a part of the nervous system that’s really important for connection and feeling calm,” Ruggiero said. Per the website, clinicians interested in bringing Skincubators to their NICUs can book a call with the company to begin a pilot program. Learn more. items.description: Ένας βραχίονας ρομπότ που λυγίζει σαν τον κορμό ελέφαντα μπορεί να γλιστρήσει σε στενούς χώρους και να χειριστεί εύθραυστα αντικείμενα. Ο έλεγχος του είναι πιο δύσκολος επειδή η ομαλή κάμψη του κάνει την επόμενη κίνησή του δύσκολο να προβλεφθεί. Οι ερευνητές ανέπτυξαν τώρα μια μέθοδο που διατηρεί τις προβλέψεις του υπολογιστή για την κίνηση του χεριού σε καλό δρόμο, ακόμη και όταν ο βραχίονας κινείται πιο γρήγορα από ό,τι το μοντέλο ήταν εκπαιδευμένο…
items.descriptionOriginal: A robot arm that bends like an elephant's trunk can slip into tight spaces and handle fragile objects. Controlling it is harder because its smooth bending makes its next move hard to predict. Researchers have now developed a method that keeps computer predictions of the arm's motion on track, even when the arm moves faster than the model was trained for.

items.descriptionOriginal: “Aha!” moments are great for solving problems but less so for creative judgements, according to new research. We are all familiar with the feeling of “Aha!” that accompanies the sudden realization of our next big ideas. Notably, these insights arrive with a peculiar sense of authority—you don’t just know; you know you know. Decades of research suggest this confidence is usually merited. Across anagrams, riddles, and word problems, solutions that arrive as a sudden Aha! are more likely to be correct than through step-by-step reasoning. Researchers term this finding the Eureka Heuristic, or idea that insights act as cognitive shortcuts, telling us that a given solution is likely to be correct, against our background knowledge. Crucially, past work investigated whether insights predict solution quality in problems with one, verifiable answer. But what happens when there isn’t one? UC Santa Barbara researchers Jacqueline McGuinness, Jonathan Schooler, Shelly Gable ,and Madeleine Gross posed that question in a recent featured article in the Journal of Intelligence . Their answer: in open-ended creative work, the Aha! experience is less a signal of accuracy, and more an illusory sense of brilliance—a phenomenon they refer to as the Aha! glow. “Insights tell us that an idea is promising, but primarily when there is a correct answer to be had,” says McGuinness, manager of Schooler’s META Lab in UCSB’s psychological and brain sciences department. “When we widen the solution space in creative contexts, the feeling of insight can inflate our perception of how good our ideas really are.” Evidence for the Aha! glow first comes from re-analysis of a daily diary study that tracked professional writers and physicists over two weeks. Every night, participants logged their best idea from the day, along with how creative they thought the idea was, and whether or not it came as an “Aha!” moment. Six months later, they were asked to rate the creativity of each idea again. These professions were chosen as real-world proxies for two types of problem-solving. Physicists tend to work on problems with a single, defined solution. Creative writers, in contrast, face problems where many ideas could work, and the value of each only reveals itself once fully developed. The findings revealed a striking difference between professions: writers rated their Aha! ideas as highly creative at the time of idea generation, but much lower 6-months later. On the other hand, physicists rated their Aha! ideas as more creative over time. So when an idea arrives with a flash of insight—an Aha! moment—writers come to think less of it over time, while physicists come to think more of it. Crucially, this divergence only occurred for insights; ideas arrived at through analytical reasoning improved slightly over time for both groups. A second study had 100 participants complete two laboratory tasks: a word problem task with one answer per problem, and the alternate uses task, where participants provide unusual uses for common objects like a brick or tin can. On the alternate uses task, stronger insight experiences predicted how creative people thought their ideas were, much more than creativity judgements of independent raters. Within the same participants, the association between insight intensity and idea quality was nearly four times stronger in the word problem task, compared to the creative idea generation task. “That’s the part I find illuminating,” says Schooler, a distinguished professor of psychological and brain sciences and director of UCSB’s Center for Mindfulness and Human Potential. “For the very same person the experience of aha is well-calibrated to the quality of their ideas on the one task, but produces an Aha! glow on the other.” Yet the team suspects that the glow remains useful. Across both studies, Aha! experiences also predicted greater task enjoyment, confidence, and self-reported motivation to continue working. “In creative work where there is no singular way of assessing solution quality, it often takes months or even years to assess whether an idea will be any good,” adds Gross, a project scientist in the META Lab. “So a boost of confidence, although not always warranted, might be what you need to stick with an idea long enough to find out.” In other words, the researchers say, Aha! moments in creative contexts such as the arts may be less a verdict than a motivational impetus—one that those laboring on ideas unfinished have reason to accept, even if exaggerated. Source: UC Santa Barbara The post ‘Aha!’ moments are good for problem solving, but less helpful for creative work appeared first on Futurity .
