items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Germany just finished building the world’s tallest wind turbine: 1,197 feet tall, and built without a crane. They had to invent an entirely new construction method, because cranes don’t go that high. Also this week: the Hungarian law that fell in the most unexpected way, a Spanish explorer crossing Antarctica on kite power alone, and why fall makes your brain reach for the same reruns every year. Ten solutions total. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Intro Arielle: Hello everyone, I’m Arielle. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. What’s new in your world, Karissa? Karissa: Well, I’m excited that this week has graced us with a little bit of rain and some cloudy weather, and it’s just really starting to make me feel pretty cozy and nostalgic, honestly. Which kind of has to do with one of our solutions later. But, uh, yeah, it’s been, it’s been good over here. What about you, Arielle? Arielle: Um, I shaved my head. Karissa: Well, that’s pretty big. Arielle: So that’s been pretty new. Yeah. I mean, obviously this is a podcast, so people don’t know what I look like regularly, but, uh, I did have hair, and now I don’t, and that’s been very liberating. Mm. But yeah, it is getting colder, so maybe not the most opportune time- I was gonna say … to have an exposed head. But, um, here we are. It’s okay. Uh, just need to get myself, like, a nice little toque, or I guess… Yeah, toque is such a Canadian word, but it’s basically just, like, a beanie. So yeah, I’ll be in the market for some cozy little beanies. But yeah, other than that, nothing really crazy to report. Karissa: Well, that’s a really big change and a very exciting one. Hmm. Um- And it kind of goes with, like, the changing of the seasons as well, so that’s, uh- Yeah. I love it. Arielle: Yeah. The, the, the trees are shedding their leaves, and so am I, in a way. Karissa: Yes. You are also shedding the season away and starting anew. I love it. Arielle: Yeah. And as you said, Karissa, some of our solutions have to do with, uh, changing seasons and nostalgia and all of that. Newsletter & Socials Arielle: But before we get into the solutions, we would love to remind everyone that they can sign up for our free daily or weekly newsletter. You can find the link to sign up for that in the show notes, and that way you’ll get all of this positive news straight to your inbox. Karissa: You can also get all of this positive news on our social media feeds. You can follow us at @optimistdaily on basically everything, except on X, where we are @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: We love it when you guys engage with us, like our stories or posts, share with friends and family, or just on your own personal stories. All of that is really, really appreciated. Your comments, questions, feedback is very welcome. Or you can reach Karissa and I directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Sharing these solutions in any way possible really helps us out with our mission, and it’s a free way to help The Optimist Daily. But if you’d like to financially support The Optimist Daily, then you can become an Emissary. The link to do that is in the show notes. And Emissaries also get a really cool podcast shout-out to someone or something that makes you optimistic if you sign up. That email with the information on how to do that should automatically go to you, and we send out periodic reminders as well to- Submit your shout-outs. Emissary Shout-out & Local Changemakers Arielle: Yeah, we haven’t really mentioned the Emissary Shout-out recently, because we’ve been focusing on our Local Changemakers series. On that note, we would love to thank everyone who participated and nominated, uh, young local changemakers. This year, we were focusing on changemakers who are 30 years old and under. And it’s been really fun to read all of the submissions. And it has been a little bit difficult to choose our finalists. But we have them, and we are excited to share their stories with you in the coming weeks. Yeah, we’re gonna be starting to publish the Local Changemakers series next week on Wednesday. And we will be featuring a local changemaker every Wednesday into the run-up to Thanksgiving. Karissa: Yeah, I’m so excited to share these stories. And thank you once again to everyone who nominated a young changemaker. Arielle: Mm-hmm. We did get some comments that people were wondering why we were limiting the age. Um, and honestly, in the last two years that we’ve done the Local Changemakers series, I don’t think anyone who was nominated was under the age of 30. Most of the submissions were for people who had established charities or who were just further along, you know, in their lives and professional, uh, experiences. So, that’s why we decided to focus on the younger generation this year. If you wanted to nominate someone who was out of this age range, then there’s always next year for that. Karissa: And we always have our emails open for any suggestions on people to feature on The Optimist Daily. And we sincerely appreciate all of you sharing all the optimism in your own lives with us year-round. Arielle: But speaking of sharing optimism, should I dive into this week’s solutions? Karissa: Yeah, let’s get into all the positive news from this week. Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law Arielle: The first solution is titled “Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, unlocking billions in EU funds”. Hungary just repealed the law that banned any mention of homosexuality or transgender identities in schools and media, a law Orbán’s government had defended for five years as, quote unquote, “child protection.” The EU had been withholding four point two billion euros over it. And the thing that finally made the law politically toxic for the government wasn’t a rights campaign. It was actually a child abuse scandal. So the political unraveling started when Orbán’s government pardoned someone who had covered up abuse at a children’s home, which turned their own child protection law into a liability rather than an asset. The repeal went further than reversing the 2021 law. It also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe. Those are major EU research programs that had been suspended along with the funding. The civil rights organization that fought this for five whole years is celebrating, but they’re clear that this isn’t full equality yet. There’s still no same-sex marriage, no adoption rights, and no legal name change process for transgender individuals. But this is a step in the right direction, and we’re here to celebrate every win. How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem Arielle: The second solution is titled “How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem”. Most people who live in apartments, like me, have been completely locked out of the rooftop solar boom. You can’t just install panels on a building you share with, like, 40 other households. An Australian company built a device that essentially solves that, and it just won the top design award in Australia. We actually talked about Australia’s renewable energy boom last week as well. Karissa: Yeah. Yeah, another, um, win for them is how much renewable energy they were generating on one day, and a lot of that coming from individual solar rooftops. Arielle: SolShare acts as a traffic controller for solar power, automatically reading each apartment’s real-time energy use and routing power from a single rooftop system to whomever needs it. No separate inverters, no complicated wiring per unit, or any of that. Millions of people in Australia live in apartments and have basically no access to rooftop solar benefits until now. There’s been, like, a lot of talk on how to get apartment dwellers involved in solar energy generation. I know that in Spain and I think in Germany, they have these, like, balcony solar panels that you can use. Um, but this one seems even more efficient. Karissa: Yeah. Um, balcony solar is a good approach to this too, but not a comprehensive solution. In California, I know that a bill that allows plug-in balcony solar just got passed, so that’s good because, I mean, there’s a lot of apartments here in this really big state as well. So that will help. But, um, this design could help make everything more efficient. The surprising history of pumpkins Arielle: The next solution is titled “The surprising history of pumpkins: from ancient staple to autumn icon”. So here’s a, a nice, uh, seasonal one for everyone. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: You know pumpkin as the flavor of fall, lattes, and pies, and doorstep decorations, but pumpkin isn’t actually a botanical category. It’s more of a cultural idea that’s been assigned to things for centuries, and for a while in the 1600s, it was a straight-up insult. The whole history- … is weirder and funnier than you’d expect. So the word pumpkin started with the Greeks, and then traveled through French, and landed in English as pompion in the 1500s. It first appeared in print in 1647 as a reference to how poorly early colonists were eating. Not exactly a glamorous origin. By the late 1600s, pumpkin had become an insult. Depending on who was on the receiving end, it meant either conceited and full of hot air or empty-headed. Politicians were getting called pumpkins for hundreds of years, which is funny ’cause I can think of a politician that I could call pumpkin and a lot more. Karissa: I could think of many. Arielle: Um, the reason pumpkins became a fall icon isn’t really about taste. It’s about Americans leaving rural life and then romanticizing what they left. The pumpkin became a placeholder for a simpler agrarian past that was already being lost. So I know I’ve jumped around a lot in describing this article, but you’re just gonna have to read it to, like, really get the flow of the history of the pumpkin. But- Karissa: Hmm … Arielle: you know, pumpkin spice is kind of like a mood for autumn. Um- Yeah … do you have any strong feelings about pumpkins? Karissa: Um, I am just, like, a neutralist when it comes to pumpkin spice, pumpkin-flavored stuff. Like, I think it’s good, but I don’t really, like… I’m not a huge, uh, fan and craving it all year long. When it’s here, it’s here, and I think it’s great, and I’ll grab it sometimes and maybe make something pumpkin flavored. But yeah, I’m just kind of a neutralist. What about you? Arielle: Um, I… Well, now I’m in the Netherlands, and they don’t really have this, like, big pumpkin patch culture in fall. Like, you know when, when people go pick out their pumpkins, and they bring their, like, little babies, and they have… They’re in the field, and da, da, da. I kind of miss that, so I feel like I’m- Hmm … kind of romanticizing the whole pumpkin thing- … uh, just because it’s something that I feel like I’ve lost coming to Europe. But I’m not a huge fan of pumpkin spice, if I’m being honest. I like pumpkin pie. Karissa: Yes, delicious. Arielle: Yeah. Karissa: I love the point you made about, um, you know, the pumpkin patches, being able to go to small family farms. Because those local farms, they get a real economic boost from this time of year with the pumpkin season tourism. So whether it’s just taking the family to go get your seasonal photos or going to take advantage of the cool stuff that pumpkin patches have to offer, whether it’s corn mazes or pumpkin carving. I mean, I live in an agricultural area, so I’m familiar with the pumpkin patch culture. It makes me pretty nostalgic ’cause I definitely grew up doing that. And like you said, Arielle, you have to check out the article for more. A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss Arielle: The next article is titled “A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss”. A startup in the Netherlands has developed a concrete coating that grows its own moss. No soil or irrigation. There’s no structural modifications. You just apply it to an existing wall, and the moss colonizes it on its own. They’ve already put it on warehouses, noise barriers, social housing, and bridge piers in Amsterdam, and one of those applications is specifically to deter graffiti. And I actually think I’ve passed one of these, like, in my neighborhood, um, and I just didn’t realize that that’s what it was until I read this article. Yeah. So how it works is that the moss attaches through tiny thread-like structures that grip the surface without penetrating it. So you can apply this to existing facades without any structural work. It’s a coating, not a construction project. In Amsterdam, they’re testing it out on bridge piers specifically as a graffiti deterrent, which is not a use case I saw coming. Research shows wet moss cools through evaporation the same way trees do in cities, but dry moss in direct sunlight overheats, so placement and climate really matter for how well it works. Urban greening is a major climate adaptation strategy right now, and the main barriers have always been cost and maintenance, so this solution addresses both at once. Karissa: I love that, you know, it doesn’t require, like, new construction. It can just be applied to already existing structures in cities where it gets a lot of moisture, like Amsterdam. I’m sure that this can be a really great addition. World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand the reins over to Karissa is “World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany”. Germany just completed the world’s tallest wind turbine, 365 meters tall, taller than Berlin’s TV tower, which is also very tall. They couldn’t use a crane to build it because cranes don’t go that high, so they invented a new way to do it. But honestly, the most significant part isn’t the height, it’s the proposal to add thousands of these above existing wind farms without using a single square foot of new land. As I mentioned, traditional cranes couldn’t reach, so they built like a telescoping inner tower that raises itself through a surrounding lattice structure. The construction method is as novel as the turbine itself. Germany has around 30,000 existing wind turbines, and the proposal is to place taller ones above or alongside them rather than finding new land, which sidesteps one of the biggest political fights in wind energy, which is people don’t wanna give up the land. GICON, the engineering firm that built this turbine, says, uh, this design could generate roughly twice the electricity of conventional turbines with comparable rotors because winds at 300 meters are faster and more consistent. But commissioning isn’t until November, so the real world numbers aren’t in just yet. As I said, land use is one of the biggest political obstacles to wind expansion. There’s, like, a lot of not in my backyard fights that have stalled projects for years. But stacking vertically rather than spreading horizontally reframes the whole conversation Karissa: All right. Well, I’ll take it from here, Arielle. Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns Karissa: Heading back into the whole fall idea, the next article is “Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns when autumn arrives”. The urge to rewatch your comfort show every October isn’t just a personality quirk. There’s a real psychological reason your nervous system steers you toward reruns when fall arrives. Something about the season registers as a small form of loss, and your brain responds by reaching for the familiar. I mean, I’ve definitely had this feeling before. And before I go any further, Arielle, is there anything that you rewatch every fall or find yourself, uh, reaching for? Arielle: When Harry Met Sally. Karissa: Yes. That one is very, very fall indeed. Arielle: Yeah, I don’t know. I just, I love the aesthetic. And yeah, I guess I never really noticed that I always wanna watch that particular movie once, like, the leaves start to change and stuff. Karissa: Yeah. For me, I always go back to Taylor Swift’s Red album in the fall. And it’s very, like, a fall-coded album in general, but it came out in the fall when I was, like, in junior high, and it always brings me back to that time of year. And it sometimes makes me feel a little bit, like, sad too because I start missing that time in my life. In general, your body recognizes fall through a whole bunch of sensory clues. There’s wood smoke, October light, the sound of a school bus, and that’s what takes me back to Red. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Karissa: But the same memory system that holds pre-verbal experiences from early childhood is also at play here when you experience all these, these autumn, um, these autumn- Arielle: Sensations Karissa: things. Yeah, sensations is exactly the word. Psychologists say we prefer reruns in the fall because our brains favor predictability when things feel uncertain. And you already know how it ends, so that matters a lot more than you’d think. Nostalgia isn’t just about these warm, fuzzy feelings. It can also hold a lot of grief, and looking backward is a part of how we integrate the past and then move forward. So there is a psychological reason why we want to indulge in this fall nostalgia. Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Karissa: Okay, the next solution is, “Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says”. Apparently pistachios contain their own melatonin. They don’t just offer compounds that help your body make melatonin, they produce it themselves. A nutritional review found that one small handful covers five different sleep-related nutrients at once, which is a pretty unusual thing to find in any single food. Pistachios have more vitamin B6 than any other tree nut, and B6 is the co-factor your body needs to convert tryptophan into serotonin, into melatonin. So there’s a whole chain reaction happening from that one handful, and there’s a little bit more of the science behind it in the article. The thing is that there hasn’t been a clinical trial that has actually tested pistachios directly for sleep yet, and the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers, so there might be a little bit of a bias here. But in an era where sleep is kind of one of the biggest wellness obsessions right now, and there’s magnesium supplements, mouth tape, weighted blankets, people are really desperate for anything that helps with sleep. Arielle: Yeah, I really like the food as medicine angle. It’s getting way more mainstream, so people aren’t just thinking about sleep hygiene habits. They’re also starting to ask what they should be eating. And I think food is definitely underrated, especially, um, in North America as- Karissa: Mm-hmm … Arielle: as an impactful solution to some of your health issues. Um- Yeah … so even though there’s no clinical trial yet, I think it’s, it’s worth more seriously considering food as a way to help you out with whatever health or wellness issues you’re struggling with. How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration Karissa: The next solution is kind of a fun one, “How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration”. A Spanish explorer just left for Antarctica on a sled powered entirely by kites. No engine, no fuel. The last time someone made a comparable crossing, they burned through 45,000 gallons of diesel. But this sled is built on ancient Inuit design principles that this, uh, researcher has been refining for 25 years, and NASA is also along for the ride. So again, this vehicle draws from Inuit sled design and goes back to ancient indigenous knowledge. This technology is something that’s been used for thousands of years. There’s a number of onboard research projects on this kite-powered sled. One of them is a NASA study asking whether salt rocks on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. The four crew members themselves on this kite-powered sled are also research subjects. A psychologist is monitoring their isolation, sleep, and social dynamics for 85 days to generate data for future space missions. There are such harsh conditions out there, so being able to refine and use this kite technology is pretty interesting. And of course, it’s important to use sustainable science in exploration. New research identifies the exact spot where Alzheimer’s protein tangles lock in Karissa: The next solution is “New research identifies the exact spot where Alzheimer’s protein tangles lock in”. We- researchers at Northwestern and UC Santa Barbara, go Gauchos, that’s where I went, have identified the specific point on a tau protein where the misfolding that causes Alzheimer’s begins. It’s not somewhere vague in the brain, it’s the exact molecular anchor point, down to which amino acid, so really pinpointing here. And blocking that one spot in lab experiments actually stops the spread of Alzheimer’s, so this could be a very important piece of the puzzle. The mechanism that the researchers found is called dock-and-lock. The misfolded tau docks at one specific spot first, then the rest of the protein snaps into the wrong shape, and blocking just that one anchor point inhibited fiber growth in experiments. This research is part of a broader shift towards molecular level targeting in neurodegenerative disease, identifying the exact mechanism rather than trying to clear a protein broadly. There’s still a gap between, you know, pinpointing this spot and being able to create a drug that actually does something about it. But of course, the research has to come first, so we’re happy to recognize this progress. The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model Karissa: Moving on to our final solution of the week, we have “The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model”. 13 years ago, someone planted a small orchard on the corner of a shuttered school in Kansas City, and today that idea has grown into 14,000 trees across 847 orchards in 17 cities, which means that more than a million people live within walking distance of a free fruit tree. Kansas City now has more community orchards than any other city in the country. It has nearly 250 of them. The reason 80% of these orchards are still productive, which is genuinely high for grassroots urban agriculture, is that the organization didn’t just plant trees and leave them, they built a stewardship network of 1,700 trained orchard caretakers across the country. This kind of reminds me of a solution I- we just shared about, um- Some trees planted in Germany, and they have, like, a whole app in, you know- Arielle: Mm, yeah Um- So that citizens could also take care of the trees and give them water when they, when they needed it. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I love this, uh, citizen agriculture movement. So cool. These orchard caretakers operate on about a million dollars a year and only go where they’re invited. Communities have to request orchards, so the model has held up because they don’t impose the model at all. The idea is spreading across to other cities. San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York are now in discussions to join this trend of community orchards. So it’s actively scaling, and it’s a, you know, a very hyper-local solution that individual communities can focus on and implement themselves. Arielle: And it really addresses the issue of food access. Um- Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Food access equity is a real issue right now. There’s food deserts. There’s rising produce costs. There’s diet-related chronic illnesses, and this kind of a solution that you mentioned, it’s low-tech, it’s hyper-local, um, and it’s pretty permanent. I think this can address a lot of those issues. I know that urban agriculture has been having a cultural moment, but a lot of urban agriculture is focused on, like, boutique rooftop gardens, and- Karissa: Yeah Arielle: you know, not everyone has access to that. So a community orchard serving everyday neighborhoods is a different category, and I can just imagine, like, rocking up to a tree and picking a fruit off of it- … and eating it. That… It’s also so satisfying. Karissa: Okay. Well, that’s all the positive news we had from The Optimist Daily this week. Positive Quote & Wrap-up Karissa: Before we log off for the day, we have a positive quote to share with you. Arielle: This one’s from E.B. White, the author of Charlotte’s Web, one of my childhood favorites. Okay, so the quote says, “Hang on to your hat, hang on to your hope, and wind the clock, for tomorrow is another day.” We will be back next week with more solutions, but until then, we hope you enjoy your weekend. Karissa: Yeah. Bye, everyone! Arielle: Bye! The post Podcast Transcript October 23rd, 2026— Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, world’s tallest wind turbine, and why fall makes you reach for reruns first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body to deliver medicine to infections inside a beating heart. The bots, designed to replace risky open-heart surgery and ineffective IV-drug therapy to treat life-threatening heart infections, could also be used to less invasively and more precisely treat other hard-to-reach diseases, including cancer. “With just a little pinprick, you insert a micro robot and do a procedure without infection or blood loss. And you don’t need to have a surgeon operating it to get the drugs robustly, safely, and efficiently to the right place,” says senior author Axel Krieger, a medical roboticist known for creating robots that perform surgery without human help. “There’s a lot of areas beyond heart infections where this kind of targeted drug therapy and these kinds of steerable robots could play a major role. It’s really the frontier of surgical robotics.” The work appears in Advanced Materials Technologies . Each year about 50,000 people in the United States contract endocarditis, a heart tissue infection. The typical treatment is a weeks-long course of intravenous antibiotics, which often fails because the drugs are too diluted by the time they reach the heart. Doctors are then left with two risky choices—prescribing more and higher doses of antibiotics, which can be toxic, or extremely risky open-heart surgery. To get the drugs directly to the infected heart tissue, the team developed magnetically-powered robots called “millirobots,” because of their size—they’re as wide as a pencil tip or a matchstick head, and about as long as a grain of rice. The robots work in pairs. There’s one the team calls the needle module, which gently latches onto heart tissue right at the infected site. There it serves as a docking station, waiting right on the beating heart for the drug module. The drug module carries medicine to the docking station, where it magnetically docks and slowly releases the antibiotics right where they’re most needed. Both robots are magnetic and guided wirelessly by an external electromagnetic coil system that works like an MRI machine. Having two tiny robots instead of one larger one allows the device to reach tight spots in the body. The needle can remain docked while the drug module is replaced, allowing for repeat doses of medicine if needed. “Magnetic guidance is exciting because you don’t have to power the robot itself. It doesn’t carry batteries and motors,” Krieger says. “The drugs can be delivered safely, with technology like the gradients and fields in an MRI. But instead of using it for imaging, it drives the millirobots.” The researchers successfully tested the robots on phantom heart models that closely mimic a human heart, and on real porcine heart tissue. The robots traveled smoothly and autonomously, even against simulated blood flow. “We can just inject a robot with a little pill into your vein where it travels to the site, right to where we really need to deliver the drugs, and it’s minimally invasive,” says first author Anuruddha Bhattacharjee, a former Johns Hopkins postdoctoral student who is now an assistant professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In addition to eliminating the need for open-heart surgery, drug treatment with the robots could take hours instead of weeks. “Usually if you do IV drug treatment, you need four to six weeks of therapy. But with these robots the entire procedure might take 10 minutes—maybe an hour if you want to do a couple rounds,” Bhattacharjee says. “If everything works well, you go from four to six weeks of treatment to one day or less.” The team also believes the robots would be helpful delivering targeted medications to fight cancer where it’s spreading. The researchers next plan to test the robots in more realistic phantom hearts, with muscle contraction and the beating movement of a real heart. The work was supported by the National Science Foundation’s Foundational Research in Robotics CAREER program. Additional authors are from Johns Hopkins, the University of Maryland, and Weinberg Medical Physics. Source: Johns Hopkins University The post Could tiny robots replace open-heart surgery? appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: At 74, she decided to learn something new. Today, at 82, she rides a bike, drives a tractor and shares her adventures on social media! Sukhma’s journey began when a joke turned into a secret learning adventure between her and a family member. Away from the rest of the family, they practised together until she finally learnt to ride. Eight years later, she’s doing much more than riding a bike. She drives a tractor and runs her own social media page, sharing reels of herself riding. She didn’t learn because she had to. She learnt because she wanted to. Sukhma’s story reminds us that curiosity has no expiry date, and age doesn’t have to stop us from trying something we’ve always wanted to do. items.descriptionOriginal: Search any grocery store for protein-rich food that’s good for both you and the planet, and you’re buffeted by certified labels claiming organic-grown, ocean-friendly, low-carbon, fair trade, free range, or other shining attributes. These well-meaning labels can obscure serious tradeoffs—for example healthy tree nuts that minimize greenhouse emissions while guzzling scarce water, or organic meats and cheeses that spew water pollution or planet-warming gases. A health tech scientist has proposed a new solution to this problem , in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems . The paper sketches a new rating system for high-protein foods that encompasses multiple dimensions of environmental, health, and human impacts—calculating simple overall scores that can be compared across a variety of plant- and animal-derived foods. “The goal is not necessarily to create another front-of-package label, but to foster a new literacy” that enables better-informed decision-making, writes Chris Macdonald of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom. Maintaining sufficient dietary protein is a major concern when it comes to reconciling modern agriculture with future climate change. Scientists have spent years searching for new, non-meat protein sources , ranging from marigold flowers to fungi to alternative cropping schemes . But currently available non-meat foods are also high in protein, and Macdonald has found that misunderstandings about protein content are a major factor preventing people from choosing these the most climate-intensive diet? In his latest research, Macdonald is trying to provide people with information that is accurate, comprehensive, and simple, so they can make good choices on dietary proteins. He mined scientific data on the environmental impacts and nutrient contents of various foods to develop two simple ratings. A Planet Score, ranging from 0 to 16, includes measures of greenhouse emissions, water pollution, water use, and land use per hundred grams of protein. A separate People Score, ranging from 0 to 24, includes measures of cholesterol, saturated fat, sodium, essential amino acids, commercial availability, and affordability. The Planet and People scores are then combined into an overall Better Proteins Institute (BPI) score. When Macdonald applied the system to 20 foods (10 animal and 10 plant) , tofu, chia seeds, beans, and quinoa had the highest scores (30 to 36), while cheddar, mozzarella, lamb chops, and beef steak had the lowest scores (13 to 16). The highest-scoring animal foods were chicken breast and tuna, ranking 7th and 8th out of 20, based largely on their affordability, low saturated fats, low land use, and moderate greenhouse emissions. Walnuts and brazil nuts were the lowest-scoring plant foods, ranking 11th and 12th out of 20, due to their high prices, saturated fats, and water use. Macdonald views this as a starting point, which he hopes to improve over time. Affordability and commercial availability, for example, were determined within the U.K. for this study—but they will vary substantially between regions. Future versions may also contain additional factors such as fair trade, ethical treatment of workers, or animal treatment. Macdonald. “ What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI score .” Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems , 2026. image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία είναι μέρος του "How Does It Work?" — Η σειρά The Better India που χρησιμοποιεί τα καθημερινά πράγματα που βλέπετε, χρησιμοποιείτε και βασίζεστε και αποκαλύπτει την έξυπνη τεχνολογία, το σχεδιασμό και τη βιώσιμη σκέψη που τα κάνει να λειτουργούν καλύτερα. Από τα αντικείμενα στο σπίτι σας μέχρι τα συστήματα γύρω σας, αναλύουμε τις ιδέες πίσω από αυτά σε απλό, κατανοητό lan…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "How Does It Work?" — The Better India's series that takes the everyday things you see, use and rely on, and uncovers the clever technology, design and sustainable thinking that makes them work better. From the objects in your home to the systems around you, we break down the ideas behind them in simple, easy-to-understand language. Because innovation isn't always about futuristic machines or complicated technology. Sometimes, it's hiding in the things we use every day. Look at a satellite image of a cyclone, and you will see enormous bands of clouds spiralling over the ocean. What looks like a swirling mass of white clouds is actually a complex weather system, powered by warm seawater and shaped by winds moving thousands of metres above the Earth. Predicting where this storm will travel, how strong it will become, and whether it will make landfall is no small feat. Yet, today, satellites and artificial intelligence (AI) are helping scientists make these forecasts faster and more accurately, giving communities valuable time to prepare. In India, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses satellites such as INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR to monitor cyclones. In 2025, satellite imagery helped track weather systems, including Cyclone Montha, which crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm. But how do machines in space and AI models on Earth work together to forecast a storm that has not yet reached the coast? Step 1: Satellites keep an eye on the ocean The first step is observation. Geostationary weather satellites orbit approximately 36,000 km above the equator, moving at the same rate as the Earth's rotation. This allows them to continuously observe the same broad region, capturing changes in cloud formations and atmospheric conditions. India's INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR satellites monitor clouds, atmospheric moisture and temperatures to track developing storms. Photograph: ( The Week ) India's INSAT satellites use specialised sensors to capture visible-light and infrared images, as well as information about water vapour in the atmosphere. Unlike ordinary cameras, infrared sensors can measure temperatures even at night, helping scientists identify the cold, high cloud tops associated with powerful thunderstorms. Scientists look for clues such as clusters of thunderstorms, curved cloud bands and the beginnings of a rotating system. Other satellite instruments measure ocean temperatures, rainfall and wind-related conditions, helping meteorologists understand whether the environment is becoming favourable for a cyclone. Think of it as watching a storm's earliest movements from above, even when it is far out at sea and beyond the view of coastal observers. Step 2: AI learns to recognise weather patterns Collecting data is only half the job. Scientists must also work out what it means for the storm's future. This is where AI comes in. AI weather models are trained using decades of historical weather observations , atmospheric measurements and records of past storms. By studying these examples, they learn relationships between variables such as wind speed, air pressure, humidity and temperature. For instance, a model may learn that certain combinations of atmospheric conditions and ocean temperatures have previously been associated with a storm strengthening or changing direction. AI models analyse historical weather data to learn patterns in wind, pressure and temperature. Photograph: ( CNET ) It is a little like learning to recognise a familiar pattern in a jigsaw puzzle. The AI compares the current conditions with patterns it has learnt, then estimates how the weather could evolve. Google DeepMind's WeatherNext Cyclones is one example. Its model combines global weather information with historical cyclone records to forecast a storm's path, intensity and wind structure. In 2025, its forecasts helped the US National Hurricane Center anticipate Hurricane Melissa's rapid intensification and landfall in Jamaica. Step 3: The AI runs multiple possible futures Here is where the technology becomes particularly useful. Weather is a constantly changing system. A small difference in wind direction or atmospheric pressure can alter a cyclone's eventual path . So, instead of treating one prediction as certain, advanced AI models can generate multiple possible scenarios. This technique is called ensemble forecasting . Imagine a cyclone moving towards the eastern coast of India. One forecast might show it turning north, another might suggest it moving towards the northwest, while others may predict different speeds or intensities. Ensemble forecasting generates multiple possible storm tracks, helping meteorologists assess uncertainty. Photograph: ( FOX Weather ) By comparing these possible tracks, meteorologists can identify areas that are more likely to be affected and understand where uncertainty remains. WeatherNext Cyclones can generate 1,000 possible scenarios in less than a minute on specialised computing hardware. Its forecasts can extend up to 15 days ahead, although uncertainty generally increases the further into the future a prediction looks. Step 4: Forecasters turn predictions into warnings AI does not replace meteorologists. Instead, its predictions complement satellite observations, conventional weather models and expert analysis. Forecasters assess the available evidence before issuing official warnings about a cyclone's likely track, strength, rainfall and landfall. These warnings help authorities plan evacuations, fishermen return to shore, and emergency teams prepare shelters and supplies. The goal is not to predict every movement perfectly. It is to reduce uncertainty early enough for people to act. Early warnings help coastal communities prepare, fishermen return to shore and authorities organise evacuations. Photograph: ( facebook/@TheMech Mind) As satellites collect more detailed observations and AI models become better at interpreting them, cyclone forecasting continues to improve. Every additional hour of reliable warning can give vulnerable communities more time to protect homes, secure essential supplies and move to safety. A cyclone may be impossible to control, but understanding its likely path is becoming easier. And that growing ability to see a storm coming is one of the most important ways technology can help save lives. Sources: 'Cyclone Track Forecasting Based on Satellite Images Using Artificial Neural Networks' by Rita Kovord nyi and Chandan Roy. 'How Satellites Track Hurricanes' by National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service 'How we're supporting better tropical cyclone prediction with AI' by Google Deep Mind.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Provincial Tree Pageant Reminds Communities to Honour Their Big Trees Reading Time: 2 minutes Ontario’s Tree Trust celebrates a rare, century-old Cucumber Tree in St. George, honoring one family’s decades of stewardship and the community’s growing love for mature trees. In recent years, the Ontario government has significantly reduced environmental protection legislation. Increased development with minimal consequences threatens the province’s biodiversity, habitat, and once-protected natural character. But people are fighting back. Despite the current lack of legislation, environmental communities continue to raise awareness and push their cause. Tree Trust , a not-for-profit, grassroots organization that focuses on mature tree protection, is one of them. Education, advocacy, and community engagement are Tree Trust’s core values. Based in Elora, Tree Trust launched in 2019 and now extends to 12 communities, with chapters run entirely by volunteers. In addition to offering educational events like tree walks and talks, Tree Trust works with ISA-board-certified arborists committed to improving the health and longevity of mature trees. Protecting mature trees is essential to urban communities. Many are older than most community members, and these legacy trees offer immediate, irreplaceable benefits to our cities. Increased health and mental well-being, stormwater reduction, climate change mitigation, and economic benefits are all reasons to invest in big trees. One way Tree Trust does this is by welcoming the province to participate in the Ontario Tree Pageant. This engaging, inviting competition reminds the province that a love of trees goes far beyond the surface. For the past three years, hundreds of nominations have been received, special stories have been shared, and majestic trees have been recognized. This year’s esteemed panel of judges chose a tree that represents togetherness, a tree that is beloved and highlights a story of community awareness and environmental stewardship. This year’s winner is a Cucumber Tree ( Magnolia acuminata ), estimated to be over 100 years old, standing tall in St. George. This year’s winning tree was nominated by St. George resident and artist, Meredyth Kutt. This endangered, Ontario-native specimen stands among many other trees and is over 75 centimeters in diameter. Photo courtesy of Tree Trust . This tree is being recognized not only for being a unique and endangered species, but also for its history. Researchers at the University of Guelph have studied this individual for its ability to thrive outside its expected range. Some even say it is the farthest west mature Cucumber Tree in Canada. Beyond its uniqueness, this tree is celebrated as the epitome of environmental and community connection. The Kutt family, the tree’s owners, have stewarded it for over 20 years. They have cultivated a second Cucumber tree and currently support six of the original’s progeny. This cucumber tree’s story is exactly the kind of stewardship Tree Trust wants to support. The Ontario Tree Pageant gives people a platform to share special stories about trees that mean the most to them. It reminds us how connected we are to nature and that, for all these big trees give us, they deserve to be celebrated. The post Provincial Tree Pageant Reminds Communities to Honour Their Big Trees appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Don’t Throw Away Last Year’s Diyas: This Simple Trick Makes Them Diwali-Ready Again
items.description: Το Diwali είναι μια εποχή για να φωτίσουμε τα σπίτια μας με ντιγιά, αλλά το να γιορτάσουμε το φεστιβάλ βιώσιμα μπορεί να ξεκινήσει με κάτι τόσο χωρίς προβλήματα όπως η επαναχρησιμοποίηση αυτού που ήδη έχουμε. Αντί να αγοράζετε νέα χωμάτινα φωτιστικά κάθε χρόνο, λίγη δημιουργικότητα μπορεί να σας βοηθήσει να δώσετε στα παλιά diya μια νέα εμφάνιση. Η δημιουργός του lifestyle και των ταξιδιών Sharon JM Nathani, η οποία μοιράζεται ιδέες για DIY στο Instag…
items.descriptionOriginal: Diwali is a time to light up our homes with diyas , but celebrating the festival sustainably can begin with something as hassle-free as reusing what we already have. Instead of buying new earthen lamps every year, a little creativity can help give old diyas a fresh look. Lifestyle and travel creator Sharon JM Nathani, who shares DIY ideas on Instagram through her page @thatangloindiansindhi, suggests a simple way to reuse diyas from the previous year and make them ready for the festive season. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sharon JM Nathani || Lifestyle & Travel Creator (@thatangloindiansindhi) A trick to keep the wicks in place Her method involves using desi ghee and candles to prepare the diyas for lighting. She recommends heating the ghee, melting the candles into it, and pouring the mixture into the diyas before placing the wicks. This small change in the process makes a difference. Often, when the wicks are placed inside the diya before the liquid is poured, they can fall over or become crooked while filling. Sharon suggests pouring the mixture first and adding the wick afterwards, helping it stay upright and in place. Once the diyas are ready, you can add a little glitter or finely cut flower petals to decorate them. These small touches can give old lamps a festive makeover without the need to purchase new ones. Reusing diyas is an easy way to reduce waste during the festive season while making the most of items already at home. With a little effort, last year's lamps can return to your Diwali decorations, bringing the same festive warmth without adding to unnecessary consumption. This Diwali, before heading out to buy new decorations, take a look at what you already have. Sometimes, the most sustainable festive ideas begin with giving familiar things another chance.

items.title: Πώς ο «Artivism» οδηγεί την αντίσταση στο Παρίσι
items.titleOriginal: How ‘Artivism’ Is Driving the Resistance in Paris
items.description: Ξαφνικά ο Darth Vader ανεβαίνει σε μια καρέκλα μπροστά από το Hôtel de Ville στο Παρίσι. Ντυμένος στα μαύρα, κουνάει το σπαθί του σαν μαέστρος, ενώ 200 μουσικοί και εθελοντές, οι περισσότεροι γύρω στα είκοσι, ετοιμάζονται. Ξεπακετάρουν τα όργανά τους: βιολιά, τσέλο, κλαρίνα. Τότε ο πραγματικός μαέστρος, Étienne Jarrier, ανεβαίνει σε ένα πράσινο sh…
items.descriptionOriginal: S uddenly Darth Vader climbs up onto a chair in front of the Hôtel de Ville in Paris. Clad in all black, he swings his sword like a conductor’s baton while 200 musicians and volunteers, most in their early twenties, get ready. They unpack their instruments: violins, cellos, clarinets. Then the real conductor, Étienne Jarrier, steps up in a green shirt and the musicians of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde (New World Orchestra) begin to play. Their song is a poignant one — El Pueblo Unido Jamás Será Vencido (The People United Will Never Be Defeated), a Chilean protest song written in the 1970s by the composer and pianist Sergio Ortega and folk group Quilapayún. It has since become an international hymn of resistance, and the members of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde chant its refrain again and again to support the student protests in France this October, voicing their solidarity with the half million young people who are protesting high living costs and deteriorating conditions in their schools. “Music is a way for us to be heard,” says 25-year-old Jarrier, who co-founded the orchestra in 2022 “to find new ways forward.” A self-described “member of the climate generation,” the young man with the red-tinted black locks says he felt that climate activism had exhausted most avenues of protests and found it was time for “artivism,” art as a vehicle for political expression, “as a way of reaching people at the deepest level.” The post How ‘Artivism’ Is Driving the Resistance in Paris appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PANORAMA Builds Replicable Conservation Solutions Database Spanning Nearly 1,900 Case Studies Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes A decade-old platform now hosts 1,897 conservation solutions from over 1,300 contributors, turning local environmental successes into replicable conservation solutions database entries anyone can adapt. For over ten years, PANORAMA – Solutions for a Healthy Planet has pursued a deceptively simple mission: build a global community where changemakers share, adopt, and scale up what already works. Rather than compiling passive success stories, this replicable conservation solutions database structures each entry as adaptable building blocks, distilling complex projects into stepwise blueprints practitioners elsewhere can actually apply to their own contexts. The scale is substantial. PANORAMA now hosts 1,897 documented solutions from 1,327 contributing organizations and individuals across 11 thematic communities spanning restoration, species conservation, marine and coastal ecosystems, One Health, protected areas under the 30×30 framework, and nature-culture heritage sites. This solutions database aligns explicitly with major global directives, including the Kunming-Montréal Global Biodiversity Framework, the Paris Agreement, and the UN’s 2030 Agenda, translating local action into evidence that supports international sustainability commitments. What distinguishes each entry within this replicable conservation solutions database is methodology rather than mere documentation. Every solution unpacks the how and why behind an effective environmental initiative, breaking successful projects into essential components others can adapt rather than simply admire. Solutions must be practical and tailored to specific scenarios, relevant to sustainability frameworks, proven through real-world results, and flexible enough for varied environments and sectors. Recent additions illustrate this approach in practice. In Mongolia, pastoral communities facing recurrent droughts and dzud , severe winter disasters causing catastrophic livestock losses, needed climate-resilient infrastructure. The UN Development Programme (UNDP) ADAPT Project responded by establishing 48 hay and feed storage facilities across four climate-vulnerable provinces, using risk assessments combining climate, vegetation, and livestock mortality data to identify optimal locations. The solution strengthened emergency fodder reserves while improving herders’ adaptive capacity against increasingly unpredictable seasons. Around Lake Victoria, shared by five East African nations and supporting over 45 million people through fisheries, water supply, and agriculture, declining water quality made coordinated basin management nearly impossible without shared evidence. The Lake Victoria Basin Commission, supported by GIZ, developed the first-ever State of the Basin Report, combining water quality sampling at 44 stations across three countries with consultations spanning all five partner states. This replicable conservation solutions database entry identifies wetland rehabilitation, reforestation, and catchment restoration as the most cost-effective pathways toward improved water quality, now serving as a shared baseline for planning across the entire basin. PANORAMA’s replicable conservation solutions database documents how five East African nations built a shared State of the Basin Report for Lake Victoria and how a multi-stakeholder partnership restored Ethiopia’s Lake Hawassa, both now scaled into national and regional policy frameworks. Photo by David Munyasa on Pexels. In Ethiopia’s Rift Valley, Lake Hawassa faced accelerating degradation from deforestation, pollution, erosion, and rapid urbanization, pressures no single actor could address alone. A multi-stakeholder partnership uniting public authorities, private companies, and civil society applied a Natural Resources Risk and Action Framework developed between 2015 and 2020, jointly assessing risks and implementing nature-based solutions. The partnership succeeded so thoroughly that it transitioned to full government management and scaled into federal guidelines, now restoring water bodies nationwide. This replicable conservation solutions database operates through a partnership network spanning 12 organizations, including GIZ, IUCN, UNDP, GRID-Arendal, UNEP, Rare, EcoHealth Alliance, ICCROM, the World Bank Group, OCTO Group, ICOMOS, and IFOAM. Together with over 1,000 individual solution providers representing institutions worldwide, this network forms the backbone connecting grassroots knowledge to global policy forums, ensuring diverse local perspectives genuinely influence international environmental decision-making rather than remaining isolated success stories. Peer-to-peer exchange sits at the platform’s core philosophy. Rather than treating conservation knowledge as proprietary or locked within academic journals, this replicable conservation solutions database transforms tacit, hard-won field experience into explicit, shareable wisdom. A coordinator from the Fiji Locally Managed Marine Area Network described the platform as compelling solution providers to examine their own work more critically, improving quality and scalability specifically because their solutions will be judged against a global standard for replicability. The database’s cross-cutting scope extends far beyond conservation biology alone. Communities addressing gender mainstreaming, financing mechanisms, governance structures, technology for nature conservation, and geodiversity all coexist within the same searchable platform, filterable by ecosystem type from agro-ecosystems to urban built environments, and by region spanning Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and the Coral Triangle. As climate and biodiversity crises intensify simultaneously, the pressure to avoid reinventing solutions grows correspondingly urgent. This replicable conservation solutions database offers exactly that efficiency: proven building blocks from Mongolian herders, East African basin commissions, and Ethiopian multi-stakeholder partnerships, structured so practitioners facing similar challenges elsewhere can adapt rather than start from zero, accelerating the pace at which local innovation becomes global practice. The post PANORAMA Builds Replicable Conservation Solutions Database Spanning Nearly 1,900 Case Studies Worldwide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Ένας νομικός γραμματέας πήγε στο μετρό για να δουλέψει για 67 χρόνια. Κανείς δεν ήξερε ότι είχε 9 εκατομμύρια δολάρια.
items.titleOriginal: A Legal Secretary Rode the Subway to Work for 67 Years. Nobody Knew She had $9M.
items.description: Για 67 χρόνια, η Sylvia Bloom οδηγούσε το μετρό για τη δουλειά, ζούσε σε ένα διαμέρισμα που ελέγχεται από το ενοίκιο και περπάτησε μέσα από χιονοθύελλες στα 96 αντί να φτιάχνει ταξί -- όλα αυτά ενώ έχτιζε αθόρυβα μια περιουσία 9 εκατομμυρίων δολαρίων αντικατοπτρίζοντας τις μετοχές των αφεντικών της με μισθό γραμματέα. «Ήταν γραμματέας σε μια εποχή που έτρεχαν τη ζωή του αφεντικού τους, συμπεριλαμβανομένης της προσωπικής τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: For 67 years, Sylvia Bloom rode the subway to work, lived in a rent-controlled apartment, and walked through blizzards at 96 rather than hail a cab -- all while quietly building a $9 million fortune by mirroring her bosses' stock trades on a secretary's salary. "She was a secretary in an era when they ran their boss' lives, including their personal investments," her niece explained, and Bloom simply applied that same attentiveness to her own future, one modest purchase at a time. She never mentioned it to anyone - not colleagues, possibly not even her husband -- because, as her niece recalled, "she didn't think it was anybody's business but her own." What she did think was her business was what happened to it after she was gone: nearly all of it went to scholarships for students who couldn't afford college, becoming the largest individual gift in Henry Street Settlement's 125-year history. There is something clarifying about a life like hers -- the discipline kept private, the wealth worn invisibly, the generosity revealed only at the end, as if the whole thing had been a very long, very patient act of faith in someone else's future.

items.descriptionOriginal: For decades, India's growing cities have dealt with their waste by moving it out of sight. Over time, municipal dumping grounds have grown into mountains of mixed garbage, often close to homes, informal settlements and roads. But what happens when a city finally clears one of these mountains? Can land occupied by garbage for years become a park, a forest or another public space? And what happens to the people who have depended on these sites for their livelihoods? The Dumpsite Remediation Accelerator Programme (DRAP), launched in November 2025, seeks to accelerate the cleanup of 214 major legacy dumpsites across 200 urban local bodies (ULBs). These sites account for 80% of the remaining legacy waste targeted under the programme, which aims to reclaim land for productive urban use while preventing the creation of new dumpsites by September 2026. The real value of a reclaimed site will depend on what replaces the dump, and how effectively the city manages the waste it generates every. day Photograph: (Needpix) The programme covers 200 ULBs and targets complete remediation of 214 of the most challenging dumpsites across states and Union territories. The scale of the task is considerable, but the experiences of cities already working on or reclaiming such sites show that the challenge extends beyond removing old waste. It involves deciding what happens to the recovered land, where the extracted material goes, and whether the people who have worked with waste for years have a place in the new system. 1. Gorakhpur: A former dumping ground becomes an eco-park In Gorakhpur , Uttar Pradesh, a 40-acre site that had served as the city's primary waste disposal ground for seven years has been transformed into the Kachre Se Kanchan Rapti Eco Park, in September 2026. The remediation involved processing around 400 tonnes of accumulated waste every day. Instead of treating the site as a dumping ground indefinitely, the project sought to recover the land and give it a public-facing purpose. The cleared site was subsequently developed into a public space with green lawns, walking and jogging tracks, a children's play area, an open gym and a yoga zone. Solar lighting and water-conservation structures were also incorporated. According to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the park also has a livelihood component. A women-led self-help group, Shakti Ki Rasoi, operates a restaurant on the premises. The park reportedly attracts around 500 visitors daily. 2. Raichur: Reclaiming a dumpsite for green cover In Raichur, Karnataka, the reclamation of the Yakalaspura dumpsite is taking a different route. Rather than developing a conventional public park across the reclaimed land, the project includes restoring green cover. The 35-acre site has undergone scientific remediation, with approximately 62,252 metric tonnes of waste processed and nearly 22 acres of land reclaimed till 2026, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. Part of the restored area now supports a Miyawaki forest spread across approximately five to seven acres. The Miyawaki method involves planting a dense mix of native species to encourage the development of green cover. At a former dumpsite, such an intervention offers a potential ecological use for land cleared of accumulated waste. Planting trees alone does not establish that the land is free from contamination or suitable for every ecological use. Soil quality, the survival of planted species, groundwater conditions and continued maintenance all matter. 3. Delhi: Bhalswa shows why clearing a landfill takes time Delhi's Bhalswa dumpsite offers a contrasting picture. While cities such as Gorakhpur have developed public spaces on reclaimed land, Bhalswa illustrates the scale and complexity of processing decades of accumulated waste. Dating back to 1994, the landfill occupies approximately 70 acres. In June 2022, it held around 73 lakh metric tonnes of legacy waste. Biomining operations began in July that year, involving the excavation, treatment and mechanical separation of old waste into different material streams. By 26 May 2026, approximately 43 acres had been reclaimed. However, around 23.17 lakh metric tonnes of waste, including legacy and fresh waste, remained to be processed, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. The figures show that reclaiming a large dumpsite is a gradual process. Biomining involves separating recoverable materials from mixed waste, with different fractions requiring different destinations. Recovered recyclables may enter recycling chains, combustible material may be processed into refuse-derived fuel, and soil-like or inert material may be used for suitable purposes, subject to its quality and applicable environmental requirements. Even after the visible mound shrinks, the land cannot automatically be considered ready for housing, parks or other public uses. Environmental safeguards, including leachate management and fire prevention, remain important, as does monitoring the quality and stability of reclaimed ground. For communities living near Bhalswa, the measure of success is therefore not just the volume of waste removed. It is whether the risks associated with the landfill actually decline, whether fresh waste is managed appropriately and whether the recovered land ultimately serves a clearly defined local purpose. 4. Pune: What happens to the people who work with waste? Pune provides an example of how waste workers can be incorporated into a city's everyday waste-management system. SWaCH, a worker-owned cooperative of waste pickers, enables its members to collect segregated waste door to door and recover recyclable materials. Workers provide a service to households while earning from user fees and the sale of recyclables. The model grew out of organising by the Kagad Kach Patra Kashtakari Panchayat, a waste-pickers' union that has advocated for workers' rights since 1993. Although Pune's cooperative model is not itself an example of a former dumpsite being turned into a park, it offers a useful way to examine the livelihood dimension of remediation. Where new processing facilities are established, cities should assess whether experienced waste pickers can be employed or organised into cooperatives to run parts of the system. Photograph: (Sajjad Hussain/AFP) A 2025 study on Delhi's waste infrastructure highlights a related concern. The closure of traditional waste collection and sorting points, known as dhalaos, and their replacement by compactors or other facilities have affected informal waste pickers, particularly women. Some have had to use their homes for sorting and storing waste, blurring the boundary between their workplace and living space. The transition to a new waste-management system therefore needs to account for the people already working within the old one. Workers need safe working spaces, protective equipment, fair and predictable earnings, access to social security and a meaningful role in decisions affecting their livelihoods. Where new processing facilities are established, cities should assess whether experienced waste pickers can be employed or organised into cooperatives to run parts of the system. The real test begins after remediation DRAP's national target is ambitious, but the scale of the remaining work is substantial. In January 2026, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs reported that 1,138 dumpsites had been fully remediated and 1,020 were under remediation, out of 2,488 identified sites containing more than 1,000 tonnes of waste each. Approximately 15.51 crore metric tonnes of legacy waste had been processed, and 8,484 acres of land reclaimed. These figures indicate the scale of the intervention, but they do not by themselves establish whether nearby residents are experiencing better air quality, whether groundwater risks have declined, or whether waste workers have secured safer livelihoods. The examples from Gorakhpur and Raichur show how reclaimed land can be put to new uses, while Bhalswa demonstrates why remediation cannot be measured only by the visible reduction of a garbage mound. So for cities, the practical priority is twofold: deal responsibly with the waste accumulated over decades and stop creating new mountains through inadequate segregation, collection and processing. A reclaimed site is only the beginning. Its real value will depend on what replaces the dump, how effectively the city manages the waste it generates every day, whether the land is safe for its intended use, and whether the people who have long handled that waste are recognised as essential workers in the process. Sources: 'Dump Site Remediation Acceleration Plan' : By Ministry Of Housing & Urban Affairs, Published On 29 January 2026 'Waste To Woods: Raichur Reclaims 22 Acres With Miyawaki Transformation' : By Press Information Bureau, Published On 18 August 2026 'Pune Civic Body To Complete Biomining Of Waste Dumped At Uruli Devachi-Phursungi Site By 2023 End' : By Ajay Jadhav, Published On 7 April 2023 'Reclaiming The Land Beneath The Waste:Transforming India's Legacy Dumpsites' : By Press Information Bureau, Published On 21 September 2026 'The Intersection Of Waste, Space And Informality: Exploring Spatial And Livelihood Impacts Of Dhalao Closures On Women Waste Pickers In Delhi' : By Shalaka, Urban Studies, School Of Global Affairs, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar University Delhi, Published On 14 June 2025

items.title: «Το δάσος είναι το σπίτι μου»: Αντιμετώπισε τη βροχή, τις βδέλλες και τις σκοτεινές νύχτες για να ελέγξει 3000+ βατράχους για μια θανατηφόρα ασθένεια
items.titleOriginal: ‘The Forest Is My Home’: She Braved Rain, Leeches & Dark Nights To Check 3000+ Frogs for a Deadly Disease
items.description: Κάθε φορά που η μητέρα της Keerthi Krutha, T V Champakalatha, της ζητούσε να γυρίσει σπίτι για φεστιβάλ, συχνά λάμβανε μια απάντηση που έλεγε τα πάντα για την αγάπη της κόρης της για την ερημιά. "Άμμα, είμαι ήδη σπίτι. Το δάσος είναι το σπίτι μου", της έλεγε η Κερθή. Για τον 36χρονο ερευνητή άγριας ζωής που γεννήθηκε στο Τσενάι, τα δάση των Δυτικών Γκατς εκτάρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: Whenever Keerthi Krutha's mother, T V Champakalatha, asked her to come home for festivals, she often received an answer that said everything about her daughter's love for the wilderness. "Amma, I am already home. The forest is my home," Keerthi would tell her. For the 36-year-old Chennai-born wildlife researcher, the forests of the Western Ghats had become part of everyday life. After sunset, when frogs began calling from streams and insects filled the air with their sounds, she would set out with a torch, sampling kits and notebooks. Her task was to find the frogs, collect samples from their skin, record what she saw and release them unharmed. Some nights meant crossing slippery rocks and swollen streams. Others brought leeches, unpredictable rain and hours of walking. Yet these were the places Keerthi had always wanted to be. Over several years, working largely on her own, she surveyed 49 protected areas and 19 other landscapes , documenting more than 3,000 amphibians. She was searching for answers to a worrying question: was a fungus that had devastated frogs in other parts of the world spreading through India's forests too? Her research would help scientists understand where the fungus had reached in the Western Ghats and how to keep checking for it. "If frogs are dying, then it means there is a problem," Keerthi told The Hindu in 2015. "Frogs are ecological indicators." Speaking to The Better India , she traces this work back to a childhood spent learning about snakes, crocodiles and forests. It began with a childhood love for wildlife Growing up in Chennai, Keerthi looked forward to nature documentaries and filled her shelves with wildlife books. Family trips often took her to forests rather than popular tourist attractions. The more she learnt, the more time she wanted outdoors. "It wasn't something that came suddenly," her mother tells The Better India . "Nature was always where she felt happiest." Growing up in Chennai, Keerthi looked forward to nature documentaries and filled her shelves with wildlife books. In 2004, as a school student, Keerthi was selected as a Sanctuary Asia Tiger Ambassador through the Kids for Tigers programme. Visits to protected forests introduced her to people who had made wildlife conservation their life's work. Conservation began to feel like a possible future. She also volunteered at the Madras Crocodile Bank, helping clean crocodile enclosures after the 2004 tsunami. While studying for a BTech in Biotechnology at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University in Coimbatore, she joined local snake rescues, participated in wildlife estimation exercises and volunteered with conservation organisations. "Wildlife became the direction she wanted her life to take," her mother says. By the time Keerthi graduated in 2012, she knew she wanted to work in conservation. An opportunity soon took her back into the forests, this time to study frogs. Looking for a fungus in frogs After graduating, she joined a project run by the Wildlife Information Liaison Development (WILD) Society and Zoo Outreach Organisation, affiliated with the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER), Pune. The team was investigating a fungus that infects frogs and other amphibians in the Western Ghats. It causes a disease called chytridiomycosis . Scientists call the fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis , or simply chytrid fungus. The fungus attacks their skin, which frogs rely on to absorb water and breathe. In some frogs, a serious infection can be fatal. "It has resulted in the extinction of nearly 200 species of frogs globally and threatens almost 40 percent of amphibian species," Keerthi tells The Better India . The Western Ghats, one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, are home to more than 200 frog species, many found nowhere else. Although India had not seen the mass frog deaths reported elsewhere, scientists had already detected the fungus in several species. "The incidence of this disease was recorded for the first time here in 2011," Keerthi explains. "That made long-term monitoring especially important." Researchers needed to find out which forests harboured the fungus and whether it appeared in new places over time. That meant searching for frogs in the wild, without hurting them. Keerthi was ready to do the work. What it takes to survey thousands of frogs after dark Frogs are especially active at night. Following their calls, Keerthi searched rainforests, evergreen forests, shola grasslands and streams, often working until late in the nights. Even finding these tiny animals could take hours. She carefully took a skin swab from each frog, recorded its details and released it. The swabs could then be tested for fungus without harming the animals. On one of her expeditions, her mother joined her and saw how difficult and demanding her work really was. Between surveys, she stayed in forest camps. Leeches, slippery paths, rising streams and unpredictable weather became familiar parts of the work. On one visit, her mother joined her and saw what these nights demanded. "I realised how difficult and demanding the work really was," she tells The Better India . "But I also knew she was exactly where she wanted to be." For Keerthi, each sample brought scientists closer to understanding the possible danger facing the animals she had spent so long searching for. How tiny skin samples helped track a hidden threat Collecting frogs' skin samples was only half the job. Scientists also needed a reliable way to repeat these checks in different forests and compare what they found. Keerthi helped develop clear steps for finding frogs, taking samples and recording results, so other researchers could follow the same process in the years ahead. Tests at IISER Pune found that the fungus belonged to a type already known to occur widely in Asia. The findings were published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE , adding to what researchers knew about its presence in the Western Ghats. As the work expanded, Keerthi independently secured two grants from the Mohamed bin Zayed Species Conservation Fund. This allowed the surveys to reach more places and the team to continue documenting frogs. The samples and methods gave future researchers a starting point for checking whether the disease was spreading or changing over time. An unexpected discovery in the woods The forests held another surprise. While studying a disease already known to scientists, Keerthi and her colleagues helped identify a frog species that had never been formally described. In 2017, they described Nyctibatrachus mewasinghi , or Mewa Singh's night frog, found only in Kerala's Malabar Wildlife Sanctuary. Discoveries like this help scientists understand where a species lives and which habitats may need protection. But finding a species is only the first step. Understanding the threats it faces is equally important, and frogs themselves can offer valuable clues. Tigers and elephants often draw the spotlight in wildlife conservation. Frogs are easier to overlook, but they can tell us a great deal about the health of our forests. Their skin absorbs water and helps them breathe, making them especially sensitive to pollution, habitat damage and disease. When frog populations begin to decline, it can be an early warning that something is wrong in their surroundings, potentially affecting other wildlife too. "If frogs are dying, then it means there is a problem," Keerthi says. This is what makes her research so important. By identifying where the fungus has been found, Keerthi is helping scientists keep watch for a threat that could affect frogs across the Western Ghats, including species found nowhere else on Earth. For Keerthi, the forest has always been home The child who explored tiger reserves , cleaned crocodile enclosures after the tsunami and rescued snakes grew into a researcher documenting frogs and helping scientists understand a disease threatening them worldwide. Her surveys, scientific work and role in discovering a new species have added to what we know about the Western Ghats and the wildlife that depends on them. Her mother has watched that commitment carry Keerthi through long field trips and festivals away from home. "She has always chosen the forest," she says. All Pictures: Keerthikrutha Seetharaman

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Ερευνητές στο Πανεπιστήμιο Northwestern και στο UC Santa Barbara εντόπισαν ένα συγκεκριμένο σημείο επαφής στις πρωτεΐνες tau όπου ξεκινά η λανθασμένη αναδίπλωση που οδηγεί τη νόσο του Αλτσχάιμερ. Το εύρημα, που δημοσιεύτηκε στο Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, υποδηλώνει ότι ο ιστότοπος θα μπορούσε να στοχευτεί με φάρμακα που έχουν σχεδιαστεί για να…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Northwestern University and UC Santa Barbara identified a specific contact point on tau proteins where the misfolding that drives Alzheimer’s disease begins. The finding , published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , suggests the site could be targeted with drugs designed to slow tau tangle growth in the brain. How tau proteins misfold In healthy brains, tau proteins stabilize the internal scaffolding of nerve cells. In tauopathies , including Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia, tau misfolds and recruits healthy proteins to adopt the same abnormal shape. The result is fibrillar aggregates: knotted threads that accumulate and spread through brain tissue. What happens the moment a newly produced tau protein first encounters an existing tangle wasn’t well understood. To find out, chemist Songi Han and colleagues at Northwestern used nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track engineered tau as it attached to pre-existing tau fibers, watching individual regions as the process unfolded. The region around amino acid 300 stood out because it made contact with existing aggregates faster than any other site examined, acting as an initial anchor. The rest of the protein then aligned to the fiber’s structure. The team calls it “dock-and-lock”: tau docks at the contact point first, then the remaining sections fall into place. Where water comes in The anchor’s stickiness wasn’t fully explained by the protein’s structure. Molecular simulations and water dynamics experiments added a piece: the region around amino acid 300 has an unusual arrangement of water molecules that are easy to dislodge when another tau molecule gets close. That displacement lowers the energy cost of attachment and nudges the docking forward. Chemically blocking the anchor site inhibited fiber growth. Blocking other positions had much less effect. That gap in response is what gives the finding traction as a potential drug target. A possible drug target “Once you know that aggregation-prone tau proteins always have a hotspot that is first attracted to the same site of tau that is stacked to fibrils, then you know there’s always some part of the protein that you can target to neutralize,” said Han. “If you know where to block its action of misfolding, you could block it to prevent it from propagating.” The experiments used a shortened tau construct with a disease-associated mutation, not full-length tau from human tissue , so translation to disease conditions isn’t established. The anchor point’s location may also shift between tau variants and disease types. Whether the mechanism holds across different tau structures, and whether it can be safely disrupted in a living brain, are the next questions. Source study: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences- A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation Did this solution stand out?
