items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Είναι ώρα συγκομιδής στο Κάνσας Σίτι και στην Ακαδημία του Κάνσας Σίτι, οι μαθητές βγαίνουν έξω κατά τη διάρκεια του γεύματος για να μαζέψουν τζίτζιφι κατευθείαν από τα δέντρα. «Νιώθω σαν μια πριγκίπισσα του παραμυθιού κάθε μεσημεριανό γεύμα», είπε η Νόβα Χένρι, ηλικιωμένος, «επειδή βγαίνω έξω και απλά γεύομαι μικρές λιχουδιές». Τα δέντρα είναι δωρεάν για οποιονδήποτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It is harvest time in Kansas City, and at Kansas City Academy, students are stepping outside during lunch to pick jujubes straight off the trees. “I feel like a fairy tale princess every lunch,” said Nova Henry, a senior, “because I get to go out and just feast on little treats.” The trees are free for anyone to take from. That is the whole premise of the Giving Grove , a Kansas City organization 14 years into planting fruit orchards on vacant land and asking nothing in return. It now has 14,000 trees in 847 orchards across 17 cities, and more than a million people live within walking distance of one. The Giving Grove’s origin story The Giving Grove began with a small stand of trees planted 13 years ago on the corner of a shuttered public school in the Waldo neighborhood. The school has since reopened and is expanding, so the original orchard is currently behind a construction fence, but it is still there. “This little orchard we’re standing in here started a national movement,” said Giving Grove Marketing Director Sarah Sikich. “I think it’s one of Kansas City’s best-kept secrets.” From that corner, the organization partnered with Kansas City Community Gardens to spread orchards across unused plots throughout the metro, from a few trees on a school parking lot to plots with over a hundred. Kansas City now has 248 free orchards with nearly 4,600 fruit, nut, and berry trees. “I joke that Kansas City should be the city of orchards, not the city of fountains,” Sikich said. “No other city in the United States has as many orchards as we do.” Built on shared knowledge More than four out of five Giving Grove orchards remain in production. The reason, according to founder Kevin Birzer, is that the organization never just plants trees and walks away. “It’s stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it’s not really efficient for one group to do that,” he said. “So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees , how to select the trees.” About 1,700 “orchard stewards” across the country maintain that relationship. The Giving Grove offers training, workshops, help finding grants, soil improvements, pruning support, and succession planning for when stewards move on or burn out. Janet Porter, a science teacher who tends the orchard at Kansas City Academy, has found the same to be true. “They do training. They do workshops. If I ever have any questions, they’re just a phone call away.” It is not just fruit, either. The trees attract insects , which attract songbirds, which attract predators like hawks. At least one Kansas City student turned pruning experience into a job at a tree nursery. A model spreading city by city Nine years ago, a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help, and the Giving Grove said yes. Now the organization is in cities across the country, with conversations underway about San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City. Different communities want different trees, and growing in Brooklyn is not the same as growing in Utah, especially without chemical pesticides or herbicides. “Some environments are more challenging,” Birzer said. “Creating something really cool for the neighborhood, that part’s universal.” The Giving Grove runs on just over $1 million a year. Most of it comes from 1% for the Planet , a network that channels one percent of member businesses’ annual revenue toward environmental causes; corporations sometimes add volunteer labor, and individual donors fill in the rest. The organization only enters communities that invite it, and right now it is working through a backlog of those invitations. “I think people have an easy time falling in love with what we’re doing,” Sikich said. “Planting fruit trees is something everyone can agree with.” Did this solution stand out? items.description: Είναι κολίβριο, γεράκι ή σκόρος; Το κάπως συγκεχυμένο όνομα κολιμπρί είναι (drumroll, παρακαλώ) ένα είδος σκώρου που μεταναστεύει στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο και την Ιρλανδία από τη Νότια Ευρώπη και τη Βόρεια Αφρική κάθε καλοκαίρι. items.descriptionOriginal: Is it a hummingbird, a hawk, or a moth? The somewhat confusingly named hummingbird hawk-moth is (drumroll, please) a moth species that migrates to the U.K. and Ireland from southern Europe and North Africa each summer. Its moniker comes from the way it feeds — hovering over flowers like a hummingbird. Wildlife photographer Andrew Fusek-Peters captured that feeding process earlier this month in a series of stunning photos that show the 2-inch insect beating its wings at a staggering 85 times a second while drinking from a valerian bush in his garden in Shropshire, England. Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS The striking moths have been thriving in the U.K. thanks to the warm summer. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, told the BBC that 2026 was a “record year” for sightings in the country. “They’ve had a really good year this year,” he said. “Normally they would come in small numbers. We’d normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we’ve seen loads of records of them.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS Though it borrows its name from the hummingbird, this hawk-moth actually has the avian species beat when it comes to hovering speed — hummingbirds average about 50 beats per second, while the insects can hit up to 85 beats per second. (Another fun fact: Hummingbirds are native only to the Americas, and hummingbird hawk-moths only to the U.K., Europe, and North Africa.) “The hummingbird hawk-moth is a summer visitor to the U.K. from southern Europe and North Africa but can be seen in most months of the year and is a favorite garden visitor,” Fusek-Peters told SWNS. “With warmer summers, it now breeds in the U.K. and will often overwinter here and can now be considered a U.K. breeding species.” He noted that the bugs “emit an audible hum” as they hover. “It means that it can maneuver easily with its long proboscis able to delve into deeper flower stems such as red valerian.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS As for how he captured such action-packed photos, Fusek-Peters said it took time and experimentation. “I spent much of the summer photographing them and experimented with slowing down my shutter speed to capture the incredible motion and orange flash of the wings.” This article was originally written by Ed Chatterton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Reading Time: 2 minutes How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Driving more safely doesn’t just benefit road users. Many of the habits associated with safer driving can also reduce a vehicle’s environmental impact by lowering fuel or energy consumption and cutting harmful emissions . While wider developments in vehicle technology and transport policy play an important role, individual driving habits remain part of the picture. How smoother driving can cut fuel use and emissions According to Energy Saving Trust, efficient driving techniques such as smooth acceleration, staying within speed limits and avoiding unnecessary braking can help reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This means anticipating traffic conditions and maintaining a steady speed wherever it’s safe and practical to do so. Frequent acceleration and harsh braking require more energy than gradual speed changes. In petrol and diesel vehicles, this typically means burning more fuel. In electric vehicles, it can increase battery consumption and reduce driving range. Why speed, braking and forward planning matter Safe driving is closely linked to awareness and anticipation. Giving yourself more time to react to changing road conditions can help reduce sudden manoeuvres that increase fuel consumption and vehicle wear. For example, noticing traffic slowing ahead allows you to ease off the accelerator gradually instead of braking heavily at the last moment. Likewise, anticipating junctions and changing speed limits is key. Drivers looking to improve their awareness may find that utilising telematics insurance to help you be more aware of your driving style encourages more consistent habits, as many telematics systems monitor factors such as braking, acceleration and cornering behaviour. Look after the vehicle as well as your driving style Environmentally responsible driving is not solely about behaviour behind the wheel. Keeping your vehicle in good mechanical condition can also support efficiency and help emissions-control systems operate as intended. Regular servicing allows potential issues to be identified before they affect vehicle performance. Maintaining correct tyre pressures can reduce rolling resistance, while replacing worn components when required can help the vehicle run more efficiently. Drivers should also address dashboard warning lights promptly and ensure emissions-related components are functioning correctly. A poorly maintained vehicle may consume more fuel or energy than necessary. Motoring experts regularly highlight the importance of maintenance as part of environmentally conscious driving, alongside habits such as reducing unnecessary vehicle weight and keeping tyres correctly inflated. Put greener driving into the UK’s bigger environmental picture The UK’s transition towards lower-emission transport involves multiple factors, including advances in vehicle technology and public policy. However, driver behaviour still plays a role. If millions of motorists adopt more efficient driving habits, the combined effect can contribute to lower fuel consumption and reduced emissions across the vehicle fleet. While no individual action can solve environmental challenges on its own, small changes across a large population can support wider sustainability goals. The post How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Reading Time: 3 minutes How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Retail teams work across different stores, shifts, and job roles, so training must stay accessible during busy working days. Sales associates need product knowledge, supervisors need management guidance, and every employee must complete required safety courses. A dependable training platform helps meet these demands without disrupting daily store operations. A Learning Management System (LMS) brings these needs into one trackable program. The right retail LMS software also gives leaders a clearer view of participation, assessment results, and unresolved gaps, creating a practical foundation for consistent store training. The following areas outline what to consider when choosing a system. Create One Training Hub For Every Store A retail LMS gives employees one place to access onboarding, product updates, customer service lessons, and compliance courses. A retail LMS software directory helps decision-makers compare systems built for retail requirements, including mobile access, short lessons, progress tracking, and reporting. Centralized content reduces inconsistent instructions between locations and lets training leaders update a course without distributing new files manually. Store teams also benefit from clear learning paths. A new sales associate can complete orientation, point-of-sale training, and product lessons in sequence. A department supervisor can follow a separate path covering coaching, scheduling, inventory procedures, and incident reporting. Deliver Training Around Store Schedules Retail employees rarely share the same hours, making classroom sessions difficult to coordinate. Mobile access lets employees complete assigned lessons between shifts, during scheduled training time, or at another approved location. Short lessons support this schedule. A five-minute module can explain a product feature, customer greeting standard, or safety procedure without removing an employee from the sales floor for a long session. Managers can assign content by role, location, or employment stage, so each learner receives relevant material. A Learning Management System also records completion automatically. Managers do not need separate spreadsheets for each store, which reduces manual follow-up and gives regional leaders a consistent record. Keep Product And Service Knowledge Current Retail information changes often. Product lines, prices, promotions, return rules, and service expectations require regular updates. A central course library lets training teams revise a lesson once and publish the current version across selected stores. Knowledge checks give managers more than a completion mark. Short quizzes can test whether employees understand product differences, warranty conditions, or escalation procedures. Assessment results show where a team needs a refresher before a new promotion begins. Store leaders can also use assigned learning for seasonal hiring. Temporary employees receive the same essential service and safety information as permanent staff, with a clear deadline before their first scheduled shift. Track Compliance Without Manual Chasing Retail organizations must monitor courses related to workplace safety, data protection, harassment prevention, and other internal requirements. An LMS records assignments, due dates, completions, and assessment results in one system. Automated reminders help employees address overdue courses before managers need to contact each person. Escalation reports show which store, role, or department needs attention. These records also give training leaders evidence that required instruction was assigned and completed. Access controls support accurate reporting. A district manager can review assigned stores, while a store manager sees the employees within that location. This structure keeps reports useful without giving every user access to unnecessary information. Use Reports To Improve Store Performance Completion data helps leaders measure participation, but useful reporting goes further. Scores, attempts, time spent, and course status reveal whether employees understood the material or rushed through it. Training leaders can compare results by location or role to find recurring gaps. If several stores perform poorly on a product assessment, the lesson needs clearer explanations or better examples. If one location has low completion rates, managers can review scheduling, communication, or access problems. Learning data also supports regular management routines. Regional leaders can review a monthly report, discuss overdue assignments with store managers, and adjust upcoming training according to business needs. Give Managers A Practical Coaching Tool An LMS supports daily coaching when managers connect online lessons with store activity. After an employee completes a customer service module, a supervisor can observe a customer interaction and discuss the result privately. Managers can assign refresher lessons after an observed gap. They can also recognize completed development paths during one-on-one meetings and use assessment results to plan the next coaching conversation. This approach keeps training connected to job behavior. Employees receive instruction, practice the skill, and discuss progress with a manager instead of treating courses as isolated administrative tasks. Conclusion Retail LMS software gives store teams a shared training structure without forcing every employee into the same schedule. The strongest implementation starts with role-based learning paths, mobile-friendly lessons, current product content, and compliance tracking. Training leaders should audit existing courses, group them by role and store need, then select a system that reports completion and assessment results clearly. A small pilot across several locations provides useful evidence before wider deployment. The post How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable Reading Time: 5 minutes How Schools And Universities Can Make Campus Events More Sustainable There are events across the entire school/university year for students that cover everything from orientation to graduation, conferences and cultural festivals, sports competitions. These events gather people together, but they also produce extensive waste disposable food containers, printed materials, decorations and single-use supplies for the event. Educational institutions can also lower their carbon footprint by implementing greener practices, because it also teaches students sustainable habits that they will take with them through the rest of their lives after graduation. Sustainable changes to campus events do not necessarily require a large amount of money or radical alterations. Many of the most helpful changes grow out of responsible planning, smart purchasing and greater engagement from the campus community. Think Of Events With Preventive Waste Sustainability needs to be planned in since the earliest stages of planning an event rather than being afterthought once waste is already generated. Organisers can start by estimated attendance, main supplies need to get for use and reference the environmental concern with previous events. Digital registration, electronic invitations and online event schedules are opportunities to eliminate the fabric of waste by cutting out unnecessary paper consumption. For printable materials which are necessary, organizers can print only the copies needed and use double-sided printing when they should be. Also, some schools or universities create sustainability checklists that include catering, transport, energy use and waste management. Clear responsibilities for event teams allow environmentally-sensitive matters to remain part of the planning process. Bottom line prevention from unnecessary consumption tends to work better than fully relying on recycling or disposal systems post-event. Minimize Usage of Single Use Plastics and Disposable Materials But disposable cups, plastic cutlery, food containers and water bottles are other elements of the large waste generated on an important campus meeting. A practical solution would be to offer refill water stations and promote the audience to bring reusable bottles. In places where catering facilities are present, reusable plates, cups and cutleries can take the place of disposable ones. Now when organizing the event, one should count on all the required water, energy as well as cleaning and logistics that are needed to handle reusable items properly. Easily identifiable waste stations are another effective way in which to help participants sort recyclables, general rubbish and food scraps. Such stations would need to mirror local collection and processing facilities available to residents. As there is no appropriate infrastructure, items labelled recyclable or compostable are not necessarily recycled or composted. Prevent unnecessary waste and ensure unavoidable waste is managed properly. Opt For Eco-Friendly Supplies And Materials Another consideration is your event materials. Banners, decorations, name badges, lanyards and exhibition materials are sometimes only used for a limited time before ending up in the bin, even though they can remain in good condition. By selecting durable supplies that can be stored and used again for future events, institutions can minimize this waste. With reusable signage, interchangeable name inserts and returnable badge holders, the need to buy replacements for each event can be limited. Organizers planning student orientations or academic conferences can review the reusable badge and lanyard options available through suppliers such as 4inlanyards when evaluating event identification materials. The broader environmental priority should be to select suitable products, recover them after each event, and reuse them wherever practical. Material composition also matters. Making polyester using recycled PET plastic is a way of reducing the need for virgin polyester, but there are many factors that define the environmental benefits over the whole lifecycle including how it is produced, the length of each product life and end-of-life options. Natural fibres themselves can have environmental impacts involving the cultivation of raw materials, consumption of water, post-harvest processing and transport. Instead of expecting that a single sort of material will always be the most sustainable alternative, institutions should assess durability, practicality, sourcing and end-of-life together. Environmental Initiatives for Campus Catering Food waste is a widespread problem during conferences, student parties and university-wide events. Ordering too much leads to waste, wasting not only the food but also all the resources spent to produce, deliver, and prepare it. By analyzing registration data, organizers can better prepare catering by accurately predicting expected attendance and adapting amounts to the timing of the event. Knowledge, practices and behaviour Change sProviding food that is rich in plant ingredients also can have a positive impact on the environment footprint of catering although this will vary with different components and production methods. Subject to local regulations and food safety and suitability requirements, eligible surplus food may be donated to community groups. Inappropriate collection systems may make even unavoidable food scraps unrecyclable, although these might otherwise be compostable. Institutions can record quantities of food leftovers after an event, which can potentially improve catering estimates for future events and identify sources of recurring waste. Promote Sustainable Transport and EnergyUse Individual travel by car to events over long distances can be a major aspect of the carbon footprint for campus events. Where practical and feasible, universities can promote the use of public transport, walking, cycling and carpooling. Depressingly, taking venues closer to public transport links might also reduce the emissions from travel as well. Energy consumption deserves similar attention. Organizers can have efficient lighting, switch off obsolete equipment, choose rooms according to attendance that are not unnecessarily large and so avoid heating large, empty spaces. Hybrid participation may be appropriate for certain conferences where the reduction in long-distance travel is not outweighed by a disproportionate extra energy use, nor does it exclude people who benefit from attending in person. Such decisions illustrate that event sustainability goes well beyond the materials used on the day. Get Students, Teacher, and the Campus Community Sharing responsibility for being environmentally responsible is what helps sustainable events succeed. Societies on campus, environmental groups, teams from facilities and event volunteers can all help with planning and implementation. They can assist attendees in finding out where they can refill, return reusable items , and sort the waste properly. Student groups can also hold environmental awareness sessions where it explains the reason that such practices are important. Feedback is equally valuable. Holding short post-event surveys can help determine if recycling stations were accessible, if digital materials were available and convenient, and what restatement attendees would support in the future. Participation should remain inclusive. Sustainability programmes must also take account of disabled people, financial inequalities and different access to transport or reusable products. Students engage more in these developments and are likely to continue these routines when practiced. Metrics for Better Future Events Institutions require measurable knowledge to comprehend if their sustainability endeavors are effective. Useful indicators comprise waste generation, food surplus and left over contrary to advice by the industry (i.e.feedback) as well as recovered reusable items and low-impact transportation mode-share. This allows organizers to compare the results of similar events and record which actions made a real difference. It can be something as simple as showing a post-event review that identifies the opportunity to reduce excess orders or enhance waste collection. Environmental reporting should remain transparent. Do not claim that an event is entirely sustainable based on a singular action particularly, as we have seen above where other impacts remain unmeasured or poorly-evaluated. Having a history over time for tracking progress against these targets makes it more likely that schools will set realistic targets and use them to guide decision-making. Final Thoughts Pragmatic choices to reduce waste encouraging printing less, reusing what can be reused again, the selective planning of catering and reducing travel unnecessarily are fundamental ways in making campus buildings and events environmentally sustainable while involving a wider audience on campus. The place to begin can be small steps, monitor outcomes and continuously enhance later on. These initiatives not only lessen environmental impacts but they also create an opportunity to implement practical experience relative to sustainability. Exposure to responsible resource use in everyday campus operations can shape student behavior as they move into their careers and communities. items.descriptionOriginal: At 5 AM, while Kolkata sleeps, a 74-year-old woman is busy spreading happiness, one doorstep at a time. Meet Ratnabali Ghosh, lovingly known as Kolkata’s Alpona Didi. Every year, just before Diwali, she steps out early in the morning to paint beautiful traditional alponas outside strangers’ homes, turning ordinary doorsteps into heartwarming surprises. For elderly residents living away from their children, these intricate patterns mean much more than art. They bring a sense of connection, care, and the comforting feeling that someone is thinking of them. Through this simple yet beautiful gesture, Ratnabali is keeping Bengal’s traditional alpona art alive while bringing smiles to people across Kolkata. Her story reminds us that making a difference doesn’t always require grand gestures. items.title: Πώς ο μισθός 4000 Rs/μήνα και μια δουλειά πίσω από την κάμερα ξεκίνησαν το ταξίδι του Nani στο "Natural Star"
items.titleOriginal: How Rs 4000/Month Salary & a Job Behind the Camera Started Nani’s Journey to ‘Natural Star’
items.description: «Μου δόθηκε σε χαρτονομίσματα των 100 Rs και θυμάμαι ότι τα ένιωθα στην τσέπη μου καθώς πήγαινα με το ποδήλατό μου πίσω στο σπίτι». Έτσι περιέγραψε ο Νάνι τον πρώτο του μισθό ως βοηθός σκηνοθέτη σε μια συνέντευξη που επισκέφτηκε αργότερα ο Κοίμος, και το ποσό ήταν 4.000 Rs. Είπε ότι ένιωθε αρκετά πλούσιος εκείνο το βράδυ για να φανταστεί ότι αγόραζε το μισό Χαϊντεραμπάντ. Σήμερα, ο άνθρωπος που μετράει…
items.descriptionOriginal: "It was given to me in Rs 100 notes, and I remember feeling them in my pocket as I rode my bike back home." That is how Nani described his first salary as an assistant director in an interview Koimoi later revisited, and the sum was Rs 4,000. He has said he felt rich enough that evening to imagine buying half of Hyderabad. Today, the man who counted those notes is Telugu cinema's Natural Star, an actor whom audiences describe as one of the industry's most relatable, and his road there began far from any spotlight. Learning cinema from behind the camera Born Ghanta Naveen Babu in Hyderabad, Nani did not set out to act. Inspired by filmmaker Mani Ratnam , he wanted to direct, and producer Anil Kumar Koneru let him join the sets of Radha Gopalam (2005) as a clap assistant. He then worked as an assistant director on Allari Bullodu, Dhee and Asthram , learning how a film comes together one shot at a time. Nani spent about a year as a radio jockey, hosting Non-Stop Nani before an advertisement led to his acting debut in Ashta Chamma in 2008. Photograph: ( India Today ) But before the camera found him, a microphone did. A friend working at WorldSpace Satellite Radio offered him a job as a radio jockey , and he spent about a year hosting a programme called Non-Stop Nani. According to The Times of India, the show made his voice familiar to listeners, although acting remained his greater ambition. The films that put Nani on the map In 2008, director Mohana Krishna Indraganti noticed Nani in an advertisement and cast him in Ashta Chamma , which gave him his lead-acting debut. The romantic comedy, a free adaptation of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest , was released on 5 September 2008 and earned Rs 6 crore as the distributors' share, so the newcomer arrived with a success behind him. Ride (2009) and Bheemili Kabaddi Jattu (2010), a remake of the Tamil film Vennila Kabadi Kuzhu, kept the momentum going, with the latter becoming a surprise hit. Snehituda (2009) did not succeed, yet Nani kept getting lead roles, and in 2012 he won the Nandi Award for Best Actor for Yeto Vellipoyindhi Manasu , directed by Gautham Vasudev Menon. Ala Modalaindi , a 2011 romantic comedy directed by Nandini Reddy, became his breakthrough. In 2012, S S Rajamouli cast him in Eega , where Nani's character returns as a fly to take revenge on the man who wronged him. The film earned over Rs 125 crore and won two National Film Awards, which showed how willingly Nani backed ambitious ideas. How he became the 'Natural Star' The nickname arrived with Bhale Bhale Magadivoy in 2015. It was one of the few small-budget Telugu films to cross US$1 million at the box office, and it became the first blockbuster of his career. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award for Best Actor in Telugu for it, and audiences began calling him the Natural Star because his performances felt so unforced. In S S Rajamouli's Eega (2012), Nani played a man who returns as a fly to seek revenge, taking on an unconventional role early in his career. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) What kept the title alive was the kind of person he chose to play. His characters are flawed people working through love, ambition, family and the uncertainties of ordinary life, so viewers tend to see themselves in them. In Jersey (2019), he played a former cricketer who returns to the game for the sake of his young son, a performance that Film Companion placed on its list of the 100 greatest performances of the decade. In Hi Nanna (2023), he played a fashion photographer raising his daughter alone, and the film became a commercial success. He also took risks with the image he had built. V (2020), his 25th film and first OTT release, cast him as a serial killer, his first negative role, and it became the most-watched Telugu film on streaming, according to Wikipedia's account of his career. The honours followed. Nani won the Filmfare Critics Award again for Shyam Singha Roy , which made him the only Telugu actor to win it twice. In 2024, he took home his first Filmfare Award for Best Actor in Telugu for Dasara at the 69th Filmfare Awards South, where he was also nominated for Hi Nanna. His next project, The Paradise , reunites him with Dasara director Srikanth Odela. For an actor who once measured success in a pocketful of Rs 100 notes, the journey suggests a career can be built one opportunity at a time, through patience, a willingness to try unusual roles, and a gift for looking like someone the audience already knows. items.descriptionOriginal: With fuel prices sky-high, the need for fuels from non-petroleum sources has taken on a new urgency. And researchers at Worchester Polytechnic Institute say they might have just the alternative source we need for low-carbon and low-cost fuel: bamboo. Bamboo could power trains, planes, and automobiles for as little as $2.75 per gasoline-gallon equivalent at mature commercial scale, the researchers calculate. The fuel would emit greenhouse gas emissions 26 times lower than conventional diesel fuel. What’s more, bamboo promises to be a more sustainable biofuel feedstock than conventional ones like corn and sugarcane. Bamboo is a grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some species growing several dozen inches in a day. Because of this fast growth rate, the US could make as much fuel from bamboo as it makes ethanol from corn while using about 13% as much land . The WPI researchers published their results in the journal Sustainable Energy & Fuels . “I think this research is especially timely and important because fuel prices are high and the transportation sector produces more greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. than any other,” said chemical engineering professor Michael Timko in a press release . “Bamboo would use different land than we are using for food production, so there is no food versus fuel trade-off. Farmers win, consumers win.” .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: How sustainable are aviation biofuels really? Timko and colleagues evaluated bamboo for biofuel production using a process called hydrothermal liquefaction. In the process, wet biomass or organic wastes are subjected to high heat and pressure. Polymer chains in the mass breaks down to form a biocrude oil. The oil can then be converted to other liquid fuel products. The researchers heated wet bamboo pulp to 300°C for 10 minutes. The process converted about 36% of its mass into biocrude. Unlike corn or sugarcane, which are the main plants used to make biofuels today , bamboo wouldn’t compete with agricultural land and doesn’t need much water or energy to grow. And compared with other perennial grasses that are also being considered for biofuel, it has very low ash content—less than 1% by weight—so the fuel-making process generates minimal waste. ”Bamboo may eventually offer industry a way to generate low-carbon liquid fuels at scale,” Timko said. Source : Timothy M. Woodard et al. Bamboo as a cost-effective feedstock for production of low carbon transportation fuels. Sustainable Energy & Fuels , 2026. Οι μέρες της περιστρέφονταν γύρω από τις δουλειές του σπιτιού, την κτηνοτροφία, τις αγροτικές εργασίες και τη φροντίδα των παιδιών της. Στην κοινότητά της, οι γυναίκες είχαν λίγες ευκαιρίες να παρακολουθήσουν συναντήσεις έξω από το h…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with S M Sehgal Foundation. For 26-year-old Anchal of Hussaini village, leaving home for a meeting was once difficult to imagine. Her days revolved around household chores, livestock, farm work and caring for her children. In her community, women had few opportunities to attend meetings outside their homes or speak to people from the village. So when she decided to join the Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise in Chhata block of Mathura in 2023, the first hurdle was at home. "They felt that the women of the house should not go out and work," she recalls. It was not an easy argument to make. Anchal had a household to run and three children to care for, two of whom have disabilities and need regular treatment. But staying at home had begun to weigh on her. "I was confined at home, and getting stressed. I wanted to do something of my own," she says. Nearly three years later, Anchal is part of the team running the mustard oil unit in her village. She earns around Rs 5,000-6,000 a month and contributes towards her children's treatment. But to get there, she first had to find a way to step outside a life that had largely been defined for her. The first hurdle was at home Anchal had completed her bachelor of arts after studying up to Class 12 in her village. Yet her education had not translated into work outside the home. "I didn't want to be confined to the house. I was waiting for a chance to step out and work," she says. Her family did not agree immediately. She had to convince them that she could work while continuing to care for her children and manage the household. She began waking early to finish her chores before leaving for the unit. The Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise was set up in 2023 with a total investment of Rs 14 lakh. Anchal joined the enterprise in November 2023. Her mother-in-law takes care of the children while she is away, and Anchal returns early whenever they need her. Joining the enterprise changed more than her daily routine. She had also been uncomfortable speaking to anyone outside her immediate circle. "Earlier, we couldn't speak freely with anyone outside our community. We hardly had any contact with outsiders," she says. That changed once she began working at the unit, alongside women she had never had any reason to speak with before. 'I was just looking for a chance to work' Preeti, now 32, arrived at the enterprise from a different starting point. Originally from Haryana, she moved to Hussaini after marriage. She had completed her bachelor of arts and taught children at schools in her village for around three years. Her father had also taught her tailoring and encouraged her to become self-reliant. After marriage, however, her days became centred on the household, cattle and fields. "I was always looking for a chance to work somewhere," she says. The opportunity came through the Shri Ji self-help group, which is linked to the National Rural Livelihoods Mission. When S M Sehgal Foundation began discussing a mustard oil unit in Hussaini around January-February 2023, Preeti became involved. But like Anchal, she first had to convince her family. Her in-laws worried about women working outside the home, what people might say and whether they could be exploited. Preeti asked her husband to come and see the work for himself before deciding. "I wanted him to understand what I was doing before I stepped out to work. If he was comfortable, I would take the chance," she says. He eventually supported her and helped convince his parents. Preeti also helped prepare the space for the enterprise , including arranging money for the electrical connection through contributions from home and their milkman. The women were ready to work. The next challenge was getting the enterprise itself off the ground. Before production, they had to win trust The Hussaini Mustard Oil Enterprise was set up in 2023 with a total investment of Rs 14 lakh. Of this, Rs 8 lakh came through the S M Sehgal Foundation's project supported by HDFC Bank Parivartan, while Rs 6 lakh was mobilised as community contribution, largely in kind. The idea emerged after a survey found that families in the area widely used mustard oil. Given the Foundation's existing work with local women, the team felt the women could run the enterprise on their own. Not everyone agreed. Chhaya Singh, 36, a field specialist in data and documentation at S M Sehgal Foundation, has worked closely with the enterprise for the past three years. She remembers village elders suggesting that the project be handed to men instead. "They believed women could not do it. That only made us more determined to prove them wrong," she says. For Chhaya, the goal was always for the women to take charge of the enterprise themselves. "We wanted women to be part of an enterprise, but more importantly, we wanted them to run it themselves," she says. "We also wanted them to see what is possible and help other women get the same opportunities." The machine at the centre of it all — an expeller that crushes mustard seeds to extract oil — was initially unfamiliar to all of them. For five to six months, the team met regularly with the women's family members, explaining what the enterprise involved and making the case for why the women were capable of running it. Once that groundwork was done, the team trained the women in financial literacy, stock management, and technical skills to prepare them for the work ahead. Five women now run the whole unit For Anchal, even approaching the mustard oil machine initially felt intimidating. "At first, I was afraid to even touch the mustard oil machine. I had never worked with anything like it before. But slowly, I learnt, and today I can run it on my own," she tells The Better India. With training from a technical expert, she learnt to operate the machine, understand the demand, track prices, and work through different stages of production. Preeti learnt the technical side too. "I learnt all the work in just 10 to 15 days because the team was always there to guide and support me," she says. The machine at the centre of it all — an expeller that crushes mustard seeds to extract oil — was initially unfamiliar to all of them. Eight women received technical training from an expert who supplied the expeller unit. The five women who run the enterprise today were among them. They learnt every step of the process, from handling mustard seeds to filtering the oil, filling and capping bottles, and even resolving voltage issues on their own. S M Sehgal Foundation supported the unit during its initial years and gradually stepped back as the women took on greater responsibility. How the women run the business today The unit is run by the Shri Ji self-help group, and decisions are taken collectively. Five women associated with this unit since its inception run the enterprise today. Kavita, the president, coordinates the group, reviews accounts, leads meetings and works on market linkages. Preeti, the treasurer, handles accounts, expenditure and cash flow. Anchal, the secretary, oversees operations, maintains registers and tracks stock, receives visitors and participates in decisions. Bati cleans mustard seeds and extracts oil , while Ritu handles filtration, filling, sealing, labelling and packaging. Between January and August 2026, the women sold 2,995.5 litres of mustard oil and 3,841.5 kg of oil cake. Their market now extends beyond Hussaini and neighbouring villages to Kosi Kalan town in Chhata block of Mathura district, as well as Mathura, Aligarh and Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh; Gurugram, Faridabad, Palwal and Hodal in Haryana; and parts of Rajasthan. According to the Foundation's latest figures, the enterprise generated Rs 6,53,980 in sales between January and August 2026. Since beginning commercial operations in November 2023, its cumulative sales have crossed Rs 24 lakh. Five percent is set aside for maintenance, and the remaining amount is divided equally among the five members. If someone does not need her share immediately, it can remain with the group and be lent to another member at one percent interest. 'Money has given me stability' For Preeti, the biggest changes can be seen outside the unit too. She has travelled for meetings in Uttarakhand, Mathura and Chhata. She contributes towards her children's school fees and household expenses and is able to save some money herself. Her family now sees her work differently. Her mother-in-law, who was initially unsure about her stepping outside the home, now cooks with the oil the enterprise produces and has come to rely on Preeti's earnings too. Even with that growing support, Preeti still seeks her in-laws' permission before visiting other people's homes. She hopes this will change with time. S M Sehgal Foundation supported the unit during its initial years and gradually stepped back as the women took on greater responsibility. For Anchal, earning has changed how she can contribute at home. Before she began working, she had to depend on her husband's income for purchases. Today, she can share those expenses, including the ongoing care her two children with disabilities need. "Earlier, my husband had to manage every expense on his own. Now, I can share that responsibility. If my children need medicines, I don't have to wait or depend on him to buy them," she says. "My biggest wish is to see my children get better. I am ready to work as hard as I have to if it can help make that happen," she says. What the work looks like beyond Hussaini The Hussaini enterprise sits within a wider network of women involved in S M Sehgal Foundation's work. The organisation has worked with rural communities for 28 years, focusing on skills, market connections and helping communities manage enterprises themselves. In Maharashtra, women in Nanda Agade's self-help group, who previously worked as farm labourers, now run a Custom Hiring Centre with its own tractor. The initiative has reduced annual rental costs by Rs 4 to 5 lakh. In Kolar, Karnataka, 389 women are shareholders in the Laxmisagara Horticulture Farmer Producer Company. 'I have a lot of hope for this enterprise' Anchal hopes to see another enterprise come up in Hussaini one day, giving other women the same chance to work and earn that she had. But her children remain at the centre of what she wants for the future. For Preeti, earning more is tied to the opportunities she hopes to give her children. She wants them to receive the best education possible and dreams of seeing them become teachers, following a path she once envisioned for herself. This is also part of why she has begun thinking about the future of her enterprise, as its growth will shape the opportunities she can provide for her children. "I have a lot of hope for this enterprise. I want to see it grow stronger so that all of us women can run it confidently on our own," she says. Both women came to the unit with fairly simple wishes. Anchal wanted space beyond a home life. Preeti wanted work that felt like her own. Both also needed an income of their own: Anchal for her children's treatment, and Preeti for school fees and household expenses. The unit is run by the Shri Ji self-help group, and decisions are taken collectively. Since then, both women have challenged what their families once thought possible for them. They have learnt to operate unfamiliar machinery, taken on responsibilities they once had little opportunity to pursue, and grown more confident in making decisions for themselves. Today, when mustard arrives at the unit , the women collectively know how much to buy, how to run the machine, how to keep the accounts, how to fill and seal the bottles and how to speak with customers. And when a decision has to be made, the women sit together and make it. All pictures courtesy S M Sehgal Foundation.

items.descriptionOriginal: For Kalpana, a woman artisan in Andhra Pradesh's Chinnapuram village, something that once clogged local waterways has become a source of income. She works with water hyacinth, an invasive plant that spreads rapidly across canals and ponds. Once removed, it was usually thrown away. Today, women like Kalpana are turning it into handbags, baskets, lampshades and other products people can use at home. "This work needs skill and dedication. Every product we make carries our effort and creativity," Kalpana told The New Indian Express . She reported earning around Rs 500 to Rs 700 a day from the craft. And she is part of a growing effort that has trained around 150 women across Andhra Pradesh's Krishna district to earn from a plant long considered a nuisance. How did a troublesome weed become a livelihood? For years, water hyacinth has troubled Krishna district's canals and water bodies. The fast-growing plant forms thick mats across the water, blocking movement and making it difficult to keep canals clear. Irrigation workers would remove it, only for the weed to grow back. But what if the material being discarded could be put to use? In October 2024, the Krishna district administration launched a training programme in Chinnapuram village, Machilipatnam mandal, to help women from self-help groups learn the craft of making products from water hyacinth. The initiative began with 50 women and involved experienced artisans from Assam, including national award-winning craftsperson Rita Das and her team. During the initial training phase, approximately 100–120 tonnes of water hyacinth were removed each month. Photograph: (newsmeter) The women learnt how to collect, dry, weave and finish the plant into products suitable for sale. The process requires patience. Once collected, the water hyacinth is dried in the sun for nearly 15 days. Its dried stalks are then woven by hand into different shapes, followed by gumming and polishing to give the finished products strength and a smooth appearance. During training, participants received an allowance of Rs 300 a day. Today, the Chinnapuram artisans produce around 50 to 60 varieties of handicrafts, including storage containers, mats, trays, handbags and decorative items. The women have also formed a society called Hyaloom to manage orders, production and income sharing. According to a February 2026 report by The New Indian Express , artisans in the group were earning an average of Rs 10,000 to Rs 15,000 a month, with earnings varying according to demand. From one village to 150 trained women What began in Chinnapuram has since expanded to other villages across Krishna district, including Chevendra, Leelagudem and Tamirisa. By September 2026, around 150 women had received training under the initiative. And the results extend beyond the products they make. During the initial training phase, approximately 100 to 120 tonnes of water hyacinth were being removed every month. With growing orders, the programme now has the capacity to handle around 150 tonnes monthly in the areas covered. According to The Times of India , the initiative has generated approximately Rs 20 lakh in combined sales and earnings, with an estimated margin of 20% after expenses, including labour charges. The products are reaching buyers through Lepakshi, which has been supporting their marketing. The district administration is also exploring opportunities with major temples, including those at Srikalahasti, Srisailam and Kanaka Durga. Women in Andhra Pradesh are converting water hyacinth into eco-friendly products, creating steady incomes while restoring local water bodies. A powerful blend of sustainability, innovation and women-led growth. 🌿✨ #AndhraPradesh #SustainableLivelihoods #EcoInnovation #WomenEmpowerment — Andhra Community (@AndhraCommunity) February 1, 2026 Even the organic manure produced through the process is finding buyers among local farmers. The next challenge is ensuring that women continue receiving orders. "The next priority is to provide regular orders and sustainable market opportunities to the trained women," Y Hari Hara Nath, project director of the District Rural Development Agency, told The Times of India . The administration hopes to expand the programme to the district's remaining 20 mandals. For women like Kalpana, the change is already meaningful. A weed that once had to be cleared and discarded is now something they can shape with their own hands and sell. And with each new order, the skills they have learnt offer another opportunity to earn. Sources: 'Women in Krishna district turn water hyacinth into source of livelihood' : By Vidya Dusi, Published on 26 September 2026 'Women turn water hyacinth into livelihood' : By Y Brahmaji, Published on 1 February 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Battery-Like Technology Offers a New Path for Capturing Carbon Dioxide Reading Time: 3 minutes A new battery-like technology developed by University of Illinois and Toyota engineers pulls carbon dioxide straight out of open air using electricity instead of heat. A new battery-like device can now pull carbon dioxide straight out of the air. Engineers built it by borrowing tricks from rechargeable battery technology. The approach could make direct air capture cheaper and easier to scale. Researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign built the device with Toyota. Their findings appear in the journal Environmental Science & Technology. The team says its method could outperform existing direct air capture (DAC) systems. Mechanical engineering professor Kyle Smith led the Illinois side of the project. Graduate students Paul Rozzi and JeongA Lee also contributed to the design and testing. Toyota researchers Chip Roberts and Tim Arthur rounded out the collaborative team. Cutting emissions alone likely will not meet global climate targets. Scientists say some carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere must also be removed. Doing it directly from open air, though, remains technically difficult and costly. Fossil fuel use keeps climbing worldwide, even as renewable energy expands rapidly. That trend makes atmospheric carbon removal an increasingly urgent complement to emissions cuts. A cheaper battery-like device could help close that gap faster. Most carbon capture technology targets concentrated sources like factory smokestacks. Open air contains far less carbon dioxide per breath than smokestack exhaust. Current DAC systems rely on giant fans and costly materials to make up the difference. Smith and his colleagues describe this diluted atmospheric carbon as a legacy problem. Decades of past emissions remain mixed into the air at very low concentrations. Addressing that backlog requires tools built specifically for open-air conditions, not smokestacks. Battery-like technology designed for open-air conditions rather than factory smokestacks addresses what researchers call a legacy problem, targeting the decades of past emissions now diluted across the atmosphere at concentrations too low for conventional direct air capture systems to handle cost-effectively. Photo by Nikita Belokhonov on Pexels. Those materials also need heating once they have soaked up enough carbon dioxide. That step releases the gas for storage or reuse elsewhere. Heating adds significant energy costs to the whole process. The new battery-like technology skips heat altogether. It relies on an electrochemical cell built from specialized manganese dioxide electrodes. A saltwater solution flows through the cell during operation. Running current in one direction makes the solution more alkaline. That alkaline solution readily absorbs carbon dioxide from the surrounding air. Reversing the current makes the solution less alkaline, releasing pure carbon dioxide for capture. This alkaline shift allows carbon dioxide to dissolve far more readily than in neutral water. Researchers describe the setup as a cation-compensated cell built around proton-intercalation electrodes. That design keeps the whole cycle reversible, much like charging and discharging a battery. Similar electrode materials already appear in some rechargeable battery designs. Applying that same chemistry to carbon capture is part of what makes this approach unusual. It also helps explain why the team compares the device’s operation to a battery. Early lab results already look encouraging for the new method. Researchers still need to prevent the device’s two liquid streams from mixing. Solving that problem should improve both energy use and overall capture efficiency. Toyota Motor North America helped fund the research alongside university grants. The University of Illinois has filed patent applications, with Toyota holding joint rights. Toyota describes the work as part of its broader push toward long-term decarbonization. Additional support came from the university’s Campus Research Board and Grainger College of Engineering. That mix of industry and academic funding is common for early-stage climate technology. Researchers say continued support will be needed to move the device beyond the lab. Full details of the study appear in a University of Illinois news release describing the project. Battery-like technology like this one add a new option to a still-young field. Some direct air capture methods use heat, while others use chemical filters instead. Electricity-driven designs like this one could offer a cheaper path toward pulling old carbon back out of the sky. Wider testing outside the lab will show whether that promise holds up at scale. For now, the results mark a hopeful early step for a technology the world will likely need. The post Battery-Like Technology Offers a New Path for Capturing Carbon Dioxide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: O ne weekend, a canvasser — let’s call her Cindy — was out door-knocking and found a gentleman at home. After establishing that he’d heard of gender transition surgeries for minors, a topic that’s become a major focal point across the U.S. in the run-up to the midterm elections, Cindy asked him where on a scale of zero to 10 his views were, where zero meant he was against banning procedures for minors and 10 meant he was in favor of the ban. “I’d be about an eight,” said the man. Let’s call him Ethan. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “About an Eight” Then ensued an open-hearted conversation during which Ethan admitted he thinks minors don’t always know what’s best and Cindy divulged that she is transgender. She went on to share her experience of how she had come to recognize she was trans — how she had felt like she was wearing a costume that didn’t fit. “I actually like clothes now, which is crazy,” she said. “Now I get to just pick something that’s me.” “Good!” Ethan replied. “That’s good.” Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “A Costume That Didn’t Fit” Only towards the end of their conversation did they get back to the ballot measure. Cindy explained that gender-affirming care for minors typically follows a multi-stage, developmentally-paced model, starting with visits to doctors and counselors with family in tow, and then “social transition,” where individuals change their name and pronouns. Personal storytelling and active listening, rather than debate, are at the heart of deep canvassing. Credit: JJ Lane / Be Lovely Photography Only then can they start taking puberty pausing medication, which is reversible, and after a couple years of that, usually from the age of 18, they can begin taking hormones to go through the puberty that aligns with how they want to live their life. “I wish that I had been able to access this kind of care when I was younger,” Cindy said. Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “I Only Have One Go-Around” At this point, she asked Ethan where he would now put himself on the scale they’d discussed at the start. “I’d probably be more like a three,” Ethan said. “Boy, you gonna have me thinking the rest of the day. I probably won’t sleep tonight!” Reasons to Be Cheerful · Deep Canvassing: “About a Three” Cindy and Ethan, canvasser and voter, are engaged in what’s known as deep canvassing, a technique of going door-to-door where the canvasser does more listening than talking. The idea is to have an open-minded, non-judgmental conversation about a hot-button issue, be it abortion, trans rights or mass deportations, and have the canvasser share their own vulnerabilities while asking questions about the voter’s life. The hope is to connect on an emotional level and find out what’s really going on for folks. The post The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Soil Literacy Education Gets a Hands-On Makeover in Europe Reading Time: 3 minutes A European Union-funded initiative is expanding soil literacy education across 10 countries, helping students and citizens reconnect with the ground beneath their feet. Soil literacy education is taking root across Europe through a project called CURIOSOIL. The initiative teaches students, teachers, and everyday citizens why healthy soil matters. It launched in February 2024 and runs for four years, making it a long-term priority rather than a one-time campaign. CURIOSOIL is funded by the European Union and led by the University of Aveiro in Portugal. Fourteen partner organizations from 10 countries work together on the project. Their combined expertise spans natural science, education, and social science, giving the literacy education effort a wide research base to draw from. The project responds to a real gap. Many people never learn how soil supports food, water, and climate systems. CURIOSOIL calls this gap soil illiteracy and treats it as a barrier to protecting land for the future, which is exactly why soil literacy sits at the center of its mission. To close that gap, the team builds education tools for different age groups. These include curriculum materials for primary and secondary schools. Teachers also receive dedicated training programs so they can bring soil science into their own classrooms. The project also produces Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) for both higher education and primary and secondary teachers. It offers online challenges and micro-credential modules for university students. Guidelines for blended and remote learning round out the soil literacy education toolkit for educators who teach outside a traditional classroom. One tool is the Soil Curiosity Kit, a hands-on activity set for classrooms, gardens, and community spaces. Another is the World Soil Museum, an app that lets users explore soil types from their phone. A guiding character named Petra leads younger students through these lessons. CURIOSOIL also runs hackathons and art competitions called Artathons. These events invite students to reimagine soil health through design and technology. Winning ideas get shared across the project’s full partner network, extending the reach of soil literacy education beyond the schools that first tested it. This approach turns soil science into something creative rather than abstract. A student who builds an app about soil health understands the topic differently than one who only reads about it. That hands-on shift is central to how the project measures its success. CURIOSOIL extends soil literacy education beyond the textbook through hackathons and Artathons that challenge students to reimagine soil health through design and technology, with winning ideas shared across the project’s full 10-country network. Photo by Anna Shvets on Pexels. Beyond classrooms, CURIOSOIL works to influence policy. The team has already published a report analyzing soil education policies across Europe. It plans 15 additional national policy briefs, along with a final EU-wide brief containing recommendations for lawmakers on how to fund and scale the campaign. The project also built a Community of Practice, a network of educators and specialists who share soil teaching methods. Anyone working in soil education can join, whether they teach at a university or run a school garden program. The network exists so good ideas in soil literacy education spread, rather than staying isolated in one classroom or country. CURIOSOIL sits within the EU Mission Soil, a larger initiative to protect European soils by 2030. It coordinates with several sister projects tackling related soil health goals. Together, these efforts aim to reach farmers, students, and policymakers with consistent, science-based messaging. The scale of the challenge is worth noting. Europe has millions of students who could benefit from stronger soil literacy education, yet few schools currently teach the subject in depth. Closing even part of that gap could shift how an entire generation treats farmland, gardens, and green spaces. CURIOSOIL marked its latest milestone at the Soils for Europe Conference, held in Coimbra, Portugal, from September 7 to 11, 2026. The event brought together dozens of EU-funded soil projects to share results and plan next steps under the banner “Healthy Soils for a Sustainable Future,” with sessions spanning soil degradation, organic carbon stocks, biodiversity, and citizen engagement. The gathering reflected the project’s broader goal of connecting research with real classrooms, not just policy papers. Soil rarely gets the attention it deserves, despite holding the nutrients that grow the world’s food . Projects like CURIOSOIL are working to change that one lesson at a time. As more schools and communities invest in soil literacy education, that quiet resource under our feet may finally get the recognition it has always needed. items.descriptionOriginal: When Liam Heneghan became a grandfather, he made a quiet promise: to be fully present in his granddaughter's life. Unlike his years as a busy father, when work and responsibilities often had pulled him away, he now devotes two full days each week to caring for his granddaughter, sharing in the ordinary rhythms of childhood. A Dublin-born ecologist, Heneghan finds himself rediscovering the natural world through her eyes -- from the wonder of a passing bird to the simple delight of exploring outdoors. Along the way, he's discovered that grandparenting offers something unexpected: a chance not only to give love, patience, and attention, but to receive the gift of seeing life anew. His story is a tender reminder that the most meaningful thing we can offer another person may be our time, freely and wholeheartedly given.

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Την τελευταία φορά που μια ομάδα ολοκλήρωσε μια παρόμοια διέλευση του εσωτερικού της Ανταρκτικής, έκαψε περίπου 170.000 λίτρα (περίπου 45.000 γαλόνια) καυσίμου για να το κάνει. Η αποστολή Wind Sled που έφυγε από την Ισπανία στις 18 Οκτωβρίου σχεδιάζει να μην χρησιμοποιήσει κανένα. Ο Ισπανός πολικός εξερευνητής Ramón Larramendi οδηγεί τέσσερα άτομα σε 3.400…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The last time a team completed a comparable crossing of Antarctica’s interior, they burned through roughly 170,000 liters (about 45,000 gallons) of fuel to do it. The Wind Sled expedition that left Spain on October 18 plans to use none. Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi is leading four people across 3,400 kilometers (about 2,100 miles) of Antarctic interior on a kite-powered platform he has been designing for 25 years, with 16 research projects running the entire way. The vehicle runs on wind and solar energy , meaning no combustion engine at all. Twenty-five years of design, rooted in Inuit tradition Larramendi has spent 25 years developing the Wind Sled and has logged more than 28,000 kilometers (about 17,400 miles) across ice on earlier expeditions while refining it. The platform is built on Inuit sled-building techniques, which is an unusual starting point for a cutting-edge scientific research vehicle, and Larramendi doesn’t try to make it sound otherwise. “The wind sled is something completely unique in the world,” he says. “This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient.” The sled is 15 meters (about 49 feet) long across four modules, capable of carrying up to 2,100 kilograms (about 4,600 pounds). This expedition is running lighter, around 250 kilograms (about 550 pounds) of instruments. The crew has 20 kites ranging from five to 150 square meters (about 54 to 1,615 square feet) in sail area, swapped out as conditions change. The sled can hit 80 kilometers per hour (about 50 miles per hour) in a strong wind; average cruising speed is around 25 (about 15 miles per hour). Sixteen research projects in terrain that rarely gets visited The route goes from Russia’s Novolazarevskaya base in Queen Maud Land, through the Pole of Inaccessibility and near the Pole of Cold, finishing at the Concordia research station at Dome C. Five scientific stations will be established along the way. The 16 projects were selected by Spain’s polar research committee, with collaborators including NASA’s Ames Research Center , six Spanish universities, and several national research bodies. One of the NASA projects is asking whether salt rocks sitting on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. Sensors embedded in the rocks will measure temperature, humidity, and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water could form inside them despite conditions that make that seem impossible. It’s the kind of question that sounds like astrobiology because it basically is. The Dinglac project will use ground-penetrating radar to map the top 10 meters (about 33 feet) of snow to track how ice layers accumulate and shift. The campaign will also sample for microplastics and chemical pollutants, test for microorganisms and viruses, and run assessments of the European Galileo navigation system . The location makes all of it harder to get any other way. Satellites and permanent stations have limited reach into this interior. “It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data,” Larramendi says. The crew are their own experiment All four team members are Antarctic veterans: Larramendi; Hilo Moreno , a polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki , a researcher at the University of Maine; and Javier Selva , a documentary filmmaker who crossed Antarctica with Larramendi in 2011-2012. They’re also research subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre of the University of Cádiz, will monitor the team’s psychological responses, sleep, and social dynamics across the 85 days. The data is meant to inform planning for long-duration space missions, where small crews face confinement and extreme isolation from Earth, conditions the interior of Antarctica replicates about as well as anywhere. “We are the experiment ourselves,” Larramendi says. “Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent.” A route designed to be repeated The point isn’t just to complete this crossing. Each return trip lets researchers compare data across seasons to track real changes in ice, climate, and polar ecosystems over time. “Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations,” Larramendi says. When the team arrives at Concordia, they’ll fly out and leave the sled dismantled at the station, ready for the return journey. The fuel comparison says most of what needs saying: the last comparable crossing burned through about 45,000 gallons. This one runs on kites and a design that’s been in development since the 1990s, and when it’s done, the plan is to come back. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Κάνετε τα πάντα σωστά την ώρα του ύπνου: μένετε μακριά από τις οθόνες μετά τις εννιά, κάνετε ένα χαλαρωτικό σκοτεινό ντους, πίνετε ένα δροσερό τσάι από βότανα στο κομοδίνο και διατηρείτε ένα αρκετά σταθερό πρόγραμμα ύπνου. Ωστόσο, μερικές νύχτες το ταβάνι εξακολουθεί να έχει την πλήρη προσοχή σας μετά τα μεσάνυχτα και δεν μπορείτε να το καταλάβετε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You’re doing everything right at bedtime: you stay away from screens after nine, take a soothing dark shower , sip on that herbal tea cooling on the nightstand, and maintain a reasonably consistent sleep schedule. Yet some nights the ceiling still has your full attention past midnight, and you can’t quite figure out why. If you’ve been treating sleep as mostly a habits problem, a recent nutritional review suggests there’s a variable you might be overlooking: what you eat in the evening. The review, published in the journal Nutrients , made the case for pistachios as a bedtime snack, and the reasoning holds up better than most food-and-sleep claims do. There’s no single magic compound, but what’s unusual is that one ounce of pistachios stacks five separate sleep-relevant nutrients at once, each arriving via a different route. That’s a rare combination to find in a single snack. Why diet is an underused sleep lever Most sleep advice focuses on behavior such as consistent wake times, a cool and dark room, or no caffeine past the early afternoon. Diet gets surprisingly little attention, even though a lot of research connects eating patterns to how well people sleep. People who follow the Mediterranean or DASH diets tend to sleep better, and both lean on nuts and legumes. That link pushed researchers to look more closely at which nutrients might be responsible. With pistachios, there turned out to be several working at the same time. Vitamin B6, tryptophan, and the sleep hormone chain One ounce of pistachios provides close to 40 percent of your daily vitamin B6, more than any other tree nut. This is noteworthy because B6 is what your body uses to turn tryptophan into serotonin, and serotonin is the raw material for melatonin. B6 also helps produce GABA, the neurotransmitter that tells your nervous system to settle down at night. The same one-ounce serving contains about 71 milligrams of tryptophan. In a survey of more than 11,000 Spanish university students, higher tryptophan intake was tied to longer sleep and a lower likelihood of insomnia. In a separate trial , adults between 55 and 75 who ate tryptophan-enriched cereal for a week fell asleep faster, slept longer, and produced more melatonin than those eating standard cereal. Plant-made melatonin, found in the nut itself Plants make their own melatonin, called phytomelatonin, and it has nothing to do with the melatonin your body makes from tryptophan. One analysis of American pistachios found roughly 18.7 micrograms per serving, which puts them in the same range as tart cherry and tomato, two foods with a reasonable body of sleep research behind them. Other analyses have found lower amounts, so the exact number varies, but phytomelatonin shows up in pistachios consistently. Magnesium, fiber, and the gut Magnesium supports melatonin production and plays a role in deep sleep through GABA activity. Pistachios have about 31 milligrams per ounce, around 10 percent of the recommended daily amount. Almonds have more (76 milligrams in the same serving), but every bit adds up. The CARDIA study , which tracked a large group of young adults over many years, found that those with the highest magnesium intake slept better and were less likely to get fewer than seven hours a night. A one-ounce serving of pistachios also covers about 11 percent of your daily fiber. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, which have been linked to sleep quality. In a lab comparison of common nuts, pistachios produced the most of these compounds. They also rank second among tree nuts in polyphenols, and a recent meta-analysis found polyphenol supplements helped people with sleep disorders fall asleep faster and sleep longer, though most of those trials used extracts rather than whole foods. The clinical trials that haven’t happened yet No study has directly tested whether eating pistachios helps people sleep better. The review draws a reasonable line through a lot of supporting research, but connecting individual nutrient mechanisms to actual sleep outcomes still requires human trials that don’t exist yet. It’s also important to note that the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers . If you already snack in the evening, a small handful of pistachios, around 28 grams, is an easy substitution to run for a week. The usual sleep hygiene advice still stands, and matters more than any snack. But if you’ve already worked through that list and you’re still not sleeping well, what you eat before bed is a reasonable next thing to look at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
